notes.-700: In this snapshot the source maps most of Europe as archaeological cultures rather than states. The kingdom of Israel had fallen to Assyria in 722 BC, so the source's 'Kingdom of David and Solomon' is shown as the Kingdom of Judah; its extent is too large.
notes.-500: The source does not map the peoples and cultures of central and eastern Europe in this snapshot, so those areas show as unrecorded.
notes.-323: The source leaves most of central Europe unrecorded in this snapshot, so peoples such as the Celts and Scythians come and go between neighbouring snapshots.
notes.300: The source splits the empire of the Tetrarchy into four parts, shown here as one Roman Empire; the Parthians had been replaced by the Sasanians in 224, so they are shown as Sasanian.
notes.400: The empire was divided in 395, so in this snapshot's changes the Eastern Roman Empire 'gains' the eastern half. That was a division, not a conquest.
notes.500: The source labels the Britons around Wales 'Western Roman Empire'; they are shown here as the Brittonic kingdoms.
notes.700: The source still shows Iran as the Sasanian Empire, which fell in 651; here it is part of the Umayyad Caliphate.
notes.900: The middle part that the source still labels the Carolingian Empire is shown as Middle Francia, following the Treaty of Verdun (843).
notes.1783: From this snapshot on, the source data draws the Holy Roman Empire as its member states, so some of these changes come from that rather than from land changing hands.
notes.1880: The source data shows no significant territorial change since the 1878 snapshot.
notes.1930: The source data labels the Soviet Union “White Russia” in this year; it is treated as the Soviet Union here.
notes.2000: The source data shows no significant territorial change since the 1994 snapshot.

byzantium-founded: Colonists from Megara found Byzantium on the Bosporus, the city that will become Constantinople.
massalia: Greeks from Phocaea found Massalia, today's Marseille, carrying Greek trade and culture into Gaul.
solon: Solon abolishes debt slavery and ranks Athenian citizens by wealth, laying the foundations of democracy.
jerusalem-587: Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon takes Jerusalem, burns the Temple and carries the people of Judah into exile.
cyrus: Cyrus II overthrows the Medes and founds the Achaemenid dynasty; within twenty years he takes Asia Minor and Babylon.
roman-republic: The Romans expel their last king, Tarquin the Proud, and are governed instead by two consuls elected each year.
cleisthenes: Cleisthenes reorganises Athenian citizens by district and creates the Council of 500; Athenian democracy takes shape.
ionian-revolt: The Greek cities of Asia Minor, led by Miletus, rise against Persia; Athens sends help, and the Persian Wars begin.
marathon: Athenian hoplites drive off the Persian expedition sent by Darius I.
thermopylae: King Leonidas, his three hundred Spartans and their allies hold the pass against the army of Xerxes I until they are overwhelmed.
salamis: Themistocles' Greek fleet crushes the Persian navy in the straits of Salamis, and Xerxes withdraws to Asia.
delian-league: The Aegean cities ally under Athens against Persia; the league gradually becomes an Athenian empire.
parthenon: Under Pericles the Acropolis is rebuilt and work begins on the Parthenon, at the height of Athens' golden age.
peloponnesian-war: Sparta and its Peloponnesian League go to war with Athens; the fighting lasts, on and off, for 27 years.
plague-athens: Plague breaks out in besieged Athens, killing perhaps a quarter of the city, Pericles among them.
sicilian-expedition: Athens sends a great armada against Syracuse; two years later it is destroyed.
aegospotami: The Spartan Lysander destroys the Athenian fleet; Athens surrenders the next year, ending the Peloponnesian War.
socrates: An Athenian court sentences Socrates to death for impiety and corrupting the young.
gauls-sack-rome: Gauls under Brennus rout the Romans on the Allia and sack the city.
plato-academy: Plato founds his Academy outside Athens; Aristotle later studies there for twenty years.
leuctra: Epaminondas of Thebes defeats Sparta with his oblique order, ending Spartan supremacy.
chaeronea: Philip II of Macedon defeats Athens and Thebes; the Greek cities fall under Macedonian control.
alexander-king: Philip II is assassinated and his twenty-year-old son Alexander becomes king of Macedon.
granicus: Alexander crosses the Hellespont and defeats a Persian army for the first time.
issus: Alexander defeats Darius III in person; the Great King flees the field.
alexandria-founded: Alexander founds a city at the mouth of the Nile that becomes the centre of learning of the Hellenistic world.
gaugamela: Alexander decisively defeats Darius III near the Tigris, and the Achaemenid Empire collapses.
alexander-dies: Alexander dies in Babylon at 32, and his generals begin carving up the empire.
ipsus: An alliance of Alexander's successors defeats and kills Antigonus I, fixing the break-up of the empire.
library-alexandria: The Ptolemies build the Museum and Library at Alexandria and collect the books of the Mediterranean world.
first-punic-war: Rome and Carthage go to war over Sicily, and Rome builds its first fleet.
hannibal-alps: The Carthaginian general Hannibal leads his army and elephants from Spain over the Alps into Italy.
cannae: Hannibal surrounds and destroys a Roman army of some 80,000, antiquity's most famous battle of annihilation.
syracuse-falls: Rome takes Syracuse; Archimedes, who had helped defend it, is killed in the sack.
zama: Scipio defeats Hannibal in Africa; Carthage sues for peace, ending the Second Punic War.
pydna: Roman legions defeat the Macedonian phalanx; the Antigonid kingdom ends and Macedon soon becomes a Roman province.
carthage-destroyed: Rome razes Carthage at the end of the Third Punic War, and destroys Corinth in Greece the same year.
gracchi: The tribune Tiberius Gracchus pushes through land reform and is killed by senators; the Republic's age of civil strife begins.
spartacus: The gladiator Spartacus escapes from Capua and gathers tens of thousands of slaves, defying Roman armies for two years.
alesia: Caesar besieges and defeats the Gallic coalition under Vercingetorix, and Gaul becomes Roman.
rubicon: Caesar leads his army across the Rubicon into Italy, starting a civil war against Pompey and the Senate.
caesar-killed: Caesar, dictator for life, is stabbed to death by Brutus and other senators.
actium: Octavian defeats Antony and Cleopatra, and annexes Ptolemaic Egypt the following year.
augustus: The Senate grants Octavian the name Augustus; the Republic gives way to the Empire.
teutoburg: The Germanic chief Arminius ambushes and destroys three legions under Varus; Rome gives up conquering beyond the Rhine.
crucifixion: Pontius Pilate has Jesus crucified in Jerusalem, and his followers begin to spread his teaching.
britain-invasion: Claudius sends an army to Britain; over the next forty years Rome conquers England and Wales.
temple-destroyed: Titus captures Jerusalem and burns the Second Temple, ending the Jewish War.
vesuvius: Ash buries Pompeii and Herculaneum; Pliny the Elder dies trying to help.
dacia-conquered: Rome annexes Dacia, and under Trajan the empire reaches its greatest extent.
hadrians-wall: Hadrian orders a wall across northern Britain as Rome turns from expansion to defence.
antonine-plague: Troops returning from the East bring back an epidemic that may kill a tenth of the empire over fifteen years.
caracalla: Emperor Caracalla grants Roman citizenship to all free people in the empire.
sasanians: Ardashir I overthrows the last Parthian king and founds Sasanian Persia, Rome's great eastern rival for four centuries.
valerian: Emperor Valerian is captured by Shapur I at Edessa, the low point of Rome's third-century crisis.
tetrarchy: Diocletian divides rule between two senior and two junior emperors, governing the East himself from Nicomedia.
milan-edict: Constantine and Licinius proclaim religious toleration, making Christianity legal in the empire.
nicaea: Constantine summons the first ecumenical council of the Church, which adopts the Nicene Creed.
constantinople-founded: Constantine rebuilds Byzantium as his new capital and names it Constantinople.
adrianople: Goths who had crossed the Danube rout a Roman army and kill Emperor Valens.
thessalonica-edict: Theodosius I's Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire.
empire-divided: After Theodosius I dies his two sons rule the East and the West; the empire is never united again.
alaric-sack: Alaric's Visigoths sack Rome, the first time in 800 years the city has fallen to an enemy.
vandals-carthage: Gaiseric's Vandals capture Carthage, taking the West's richest province.
catalaunian: The Roman general Aetius and the Visigoths halt Attila's Huns in Gaul.
chalcedon: The council defines Christ as one person in two natures, and many churches of Egypt and Syria break away.
fall-of-west: The Germanic general Odoacer deposes the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, ending the Western Roman Empire.
theodoric: The Ostrogothic king Theodoric defeats Odoacer and rules Italy from Ravenna.
clovis: Clovis, king of the Franks, is baptised at Reims into Catholic Christianity, winning over the Gallo-Romans.
justinian-code: Justinian I has Roman law compiled; the code becomes the basis of law across continental Europe.
monte-cassino: St Benedict founds Monte Cassino, and his Rule becomes the model for Western monastic life.
vandal-war: Belisarius destroys the Vandal kingdom as Justinian begins to reconquer the West.
hagia-sophia: Justinian's rebuilt Hagia Sophia is consecrated, the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years.
justinian-plague: Bubonic plague spreads from Egypt to Constantinople, killing thousands a day at its peak and returning for two centuries.
lombards: The Lombards cross the Alps and take much of northern and central Italy.
augustine-canterbury: Pope Gregory I sends Augustine to Kent, beginning the conversion of the English.
yarmuk: The armies of the new Arab caliphate crush the Byzantines, and Syria and Palestine pass to the caliphs.
ctesiphon-falls: Arab armies take the Sasanian capital Ctesiphon; within fifteen years the Persian empire is gone.
bulgar-state: Asparukh's Bulgars defeat a Byzantine army and found a state on the lower Danube, recognised by Constantinople.
guadalete: Tariq crosses the Strait of Gibraltar and defeats the Visigothic king Roderic; most of Iberia falls within a few years.
siege-717: A huge Umayyad army and fleet besiege the city for a year and are beaten by its walls, Greek fire and a harsh winter.
tours: The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel turns back an Arab army from al-Andalus near Poitiers.
abbasids: The Abbasids defeat the Umayyads on the Great Zab; twelve years later they build a new capital at Baghdad.
pepin: With papal backing, Pepin deposes the last Merovingian king and founds the Carolingian dynasty; his gift of land to the pope becomes the Papal States.
cordoba-emirate: Abd al-Rahman I, a survivor of the Umayyad house, flees to Spain and takes power in Córdoba.
roncevaux: Returning from Spain, Charlemagne's rearguard is ambushed by Basques in the Pyrenees, the origin of the Song of Roland.
lindisfarne: Vikings sack the monastery of Lindisfarne, conventionally the start of the Viking Age.
charlemagne-crowned: On Christmas Day Pope Leo III crowns Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans.
verdun-843: Charlemagne's three grandsons divide his empire; East and West Francia roughly prefigure Germany and France.
rurik: According to the Primary Chronicle, the Varangian Rurik is invited to rule Novgorod, founding the Rurikid dynasty.
cyril-methodius: The Byzantine missionary brothers arrive in Great Moravia and create an alphabet for Slavonic scripture.
edington: Alfred of Wessex defeats the Danish Great Army, and England is split between the English and the Danelaw.
oleg-kyiv: Oleg comes south from Novgorod, takes Kyiv and makes it his capital; Kievan Rus' is born.
magyar-conquest: Árpád leads the Magyars over the Carpathians to settle the plain of the middle Danube.
cluny: The Duke of Aquitaine founds Cluny in Burgundy, later the centre of a great movement of church reform.
normandy-911: The king of West Francia grants the lower Seine to the Viking leader Rollo, creating Normandy.
cordoba-caliphate: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph, and Córdoba becomes the largest and richest city in western Europe.
lechfeld: Otto I of Germany crushes the Magyars near Augsburg, ending their raids into the West.
otto-crowned: Pope John XII crowns Otto I emperor in Rome, the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire.
mieszko: Duke Mieszko I accepts baptism, conventionally the birth of the Polish state.
hugh-capet: The nobles of West Francia elect Hugh Capet king; his family will rule France for eight centuries.
rus-baptism: Vladimir I of Kyiv converts to Orthodox Christianity and marries a Byzantine princess, bringing Rus' into the Orthodox world.
gniezno: Emperor Otto III visits Poland and recognises the archbishopric of Gniezno, giving the Polish church its independence.
stephen-crowned: The Kingdom of Hungary is founded and adopts Latin Christianity.
kleidion: Emperor Basil II crushes the Bulgarian army; Byzantium annexes Bulgaria a few years later.
cnut: The Danish king Cnut rules England and later builds an empire around the North Sea.
great-schism: Rome and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other; the Catholic and Orthodox churches part ways.
hastings: William, Duke of Normandy, defeats Harold II and begins the Norman conquest of England.
manzikert: The Seljuk Turks capture the Byzantine emperor, opening Anatolia to them.
canossa: Henry IV of Germany does penance in the snow before Pope Gregory VII, the emblem of the Investiture Controversy.
toledo: A turning point of the Reconquista; Toledo becomes a centre for translating Arabic learning.
bologna: By tradition, the oldest university in Europe.
clermont: Pope Urban II calls for the First Crusade.
jerusalem-1099: The First Crusade founds the Kingdom of Jerusalem and other crusader states.
sicily-kingdom: The Norman Roger II is crowned in Palermo, ruling southern Italy and Sicily.
moscow-first: A chronicle mentions the small town of Moscow for the first time.
henry-ii: The Plantagenet dynasty begins; the Angevin Empire stretches from the Scottish border to the Pyrenees.
hattin: Saladin routs the crusaders and soon retakes Jerusalem.
constantinople-1204: The crusaders plunder the city and set up the Latin Empire; Byzantium breaks apart for a time.
las-navas: Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa
An alliance of Iberian Christian kingdoms defeats the Almohad Caliphate.
bouvines: Philip II of France defeats the English king and the German emperor, and French royal power grows.
magna-carta: English barons force King John to accept limits on royal power.
kalka: The Mongols defeat an army of Rus' princes and Cumans for the first time.
kyiv-1240: Batu's western campaign; the Rus' principalities become tributaries of the Golden Horde.
legnica: The Mongols defeat Polish and German knights in Silesia and win in Hungary the same year.
ice: Alexander Nevsky of Novgorod defeats the Teutonic Knights.
constantinople-1261: Michael VIII restores the empire; the Palaiologan dynasty begins.
marco-polo: The Venetian merchant leaves with his father and uncle for Yuan China.
vespers: Sicilians rise against Angevin rule and the island passes to Aragon.
swiss-charter: Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden form an alliance, the origin of the Swiss Confederacy.
acre: The Mamluks take Acre, the crusaders' last stronghold in the Levant.
golden-spurs: Flemish town militias defeat the French knights.
avignon: Popes reside in Avignon for nearly seventy years, a period known as the Babylonian Captivity.
bannockburn: Robert the Bruce defeats England and secures Scottish independence.
hundred-years: Edward III of England claims the French throne; England and France fight on and off until 1453.
crecy: English longbowmen rout the French knights.
plague-messina: Genoese ships bring the plague to Messina; within a few years about a third of Europe dies.
plague-florence: The city loses about half its people; Boccaccio's Decameron is set during the outbreak.
plague-paris: The plague moves north along trade routes and devastates northern France.
plague-england: It arrives through southern ports and covers England the next year.
plague-bergen: A ship from England carries the plague to Norway.
plague-pskov: The plague crosses the Baltic into northwestern Rus' and reaches Moscow the next year.
poitiers: The Black Prince wins a great victory and captures John II of France.
golden-bull: Fixes the election of the German king by seven prince-electors, a system that lasts over four centuries.
hansa: North German trading cities led by Lübeck form a league that dominates North Sea and Baltic trade.
western-schism: Rival popes sit in Rome and Avignon until 1417.
kulikovo: Grand Prince Dmitry of Moscow defeats an army of the Golden Horde.
krewo: Jogaila of Lithuania marries Queen Jadwiga of Poland, uniting the two crowns.
kosovo-1389: The Ottomans defeat a Serbian-led coalition and secure their hold on the Balkans.
kalmar: Denmark, Norway and Sweden share a single monarch.
grunwald: Poland and Lithuania crush the Teutonic Knights.
agincourt: Henry V wins against the odds, and much of northern France falls to England.
hus: Jan Hus burned at the stake
The Council of Constance executes Hus, and the Hussite Wars break out in Bohemia.
orleans: Joan of Arc turns the tide of the Hundred Years' War.
printing: Around 1450 movable-type printing appears in Mainz, and books and ideas spread far faster.
constantinople-1453: Sultan Mehmed II takes the city and the Byzantine Empire ends.
castillon: The Hundred Years' War ends; England keeps only Calais on the Continent.
roses: The houses of Lancaster and York fight for the English throne.
isabella-ferdinand: Castile and Aragon move towards union, the beginnings of Spain.
novgorod-1478: Ivan III absorbs the Novgorod Republic into the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
ugra: The Great Horde withdraws without a battle, and Rus' is free of Mongol rule.
bosworth: Henry Tudor defeats Richard III and founds the Tudor dynasty.
granada-1492: The last Muslim kingdom in Iberia surrenders; the Reconquista is complete.
columbus: His fleet leaves Palos, crosses the Atlantic and reaches the Americas.
tordesillas: Spain and Portugal divide the world beyond Europe along a meridian.
da-gama: Portugal opens a sea route to India around Africa.
sistine: The High Renaissance; Rome overtakes Florence as the centre of art (1508–1512).
ninety-five-theses: Martin Luther attacks indulgences in Wittenberg and the Reformation begins.
charles-v: The Habsburgs now rule Spain, the Netherlands, Austria and southern Italy.
magellan: The first circumnavigation of the globe (1519–1522).
worms: Luther refuses to recant and is declared an outlaw of the Empire.
pavia: Imperial forces rout the French and capture Francis I.
mohacs: The Hungarian king is killed and his kingdom is divided between the Ottomans and the Habsburgs.
sack-of-rome: Mutinous troops of Charles V plunder Rome.
vienna-1529: Suleiman the Magnificent's army is held at the walls of Vienna.
supremacy: Henry VIII breaks with Rome and becomes head of the Church of England.
copernicus: The heliocentric theory appears in print, and the Scientific Revolution begins.
trent: The Catholic Church launches the Counter-Reformation (1545–1563).
ivan-iv: The Grand Duchy of Moscow becomes the Tsardom of Russia.
kazan-1552: Ivan IV annexes the Kazan Khanate, opening the way east for Russia.
augsburg: Whose realm, his religion: Lutheranism becomes legal in the Holy Roman Empire.
lublin: Poland and Lithuania merge into the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.
lepanto: The fleet of the Holy League defeats the Ottoman navy.
st-bartholomew: Huguenot Protestants are massacred in Paris.
union-of-utrecht: The northern Netherlands unite against Spain, and the Dutch Republic is born.
armada: The Armada scatters after the Battle of Gravelines.
nantes: Henry IV grants the Huguenots freedom of worship, ending the French Wars of Religion.
union-of-crowns: James VI of Scotland inherits the English throne.
galileo: Galileo finds the moons of Jupiter with his telescope; the book appears in Venice.
romanov: Michael Romanov is elected tsar, ending the Time of Troubles.
defenestration: Bohemian Protestant nobles throw the emperor's envoys out of a window, and the Thirty Years' War begins.
magdeburg: Imperial troops massacre the city, the worst atrocity of the Thirty Years' War.
lutzen: Sweden wins, but King Gustavus Adolphus is killed.
westphalia: The Thirty Years' War ends; Swiss and Dutch independence are recognised, laying the foundations of the modern state system.
charles-i: After the Civil War, England becomes a republic.
pereiaslav: The Cossack Hetmanate on the Dnieper accepts the rule of the Russian tsar.
pyrenees: France replaces Spain as the strongest power on the Continent.
vienna-1683: John III Sobieski of Poland relieves the city, and Ottoman power begins to decline.
fontainebleau: Revocation of the Edict of Nantes
Louis XIV's Edict of Fontainebleau drives the Huguenots into exile.
principia: Universal gravitation and the three laws of motion lay the foundation of classical mechanics.
glorious-revolution: William III and Mary II take the throne, and the power of Parliament is established.
karlowitz: The Ottomans cede territory on a large scale for the first time; most of Hungary goes to Austria.
st-petersburg: Peter the Great builds a city at the mouth of the Neva and makes it the capital in 1712.
blenheim: In the War of the Spanish Succession, an Anglo-Austrian army routs France and Bavaria.
acts-of-union: England and Scotland merge into the Kingdom of Great Britain.
poltava: Peter the Great defeats Charles XII; dominance of the north passes from Sweden to Russia.
utrecht: The War of the Spanish Succession ends and the Bourbons take the Spanish throne.
nystad: The Great Northern War ends; Russia gains the Baltic coast and proclaims itself an empire.
silesia: Frederick II's attack starts the War of the Austrian Succession.
encyclopedie: Edited by Diderot and d'Alembert, a landmark of the Enlightenment.
lisbon-earthquake: An earthquake and tsunami destroy Lisbon and shake Enlightenment thought.
seven-years: Prussia invades Saxony, and fighting spreads across Europe and the colonies.
watt: Watt patents the separate condenser, a new source of power for the Industrial Revolution.
partition-1: Russia, Prussia and Austria take about 30 percent of the Commonwealth's territory.
kucuk-kaynarca: After the Russo-Turkish War, the Crimean Khanate breaks away from the Ottomans.
crimea-1783: Catherine II incorporates Crimea into the Russian Empire.
louis-xvi: France enters the Jacobin Reign of Terror.
partition-3: The Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth disappears from the map.
nile: Nelson destroys the French fleet at Aboukir Bay, stranding Napoleon in Egypt.
united-kingdom: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
The Irish Parliament is abolished and Ireland joins the United Kingdom.
napoleon-emperor: The First French Empire is founded.
trafalgar: The British fleet defeats the Franco-Spanish fleet and secures command of the sea.
austerlitz: Napoleon defeats the Russians and Austrians at the Battle of the Three Emperors.
hre-dissolved: End of the Holy Roman Empire
Francis II gives up the imperial title, ending an empire of more than 800 years.
dos-de-mayo: Madrid rises against French occupation, and the Peninsular War begins.
borodino: Napoleon enters Moscow but must retreat; his army of 600,000 is almost destroyed.
leipzig: In the Battle of the Nations, the allies decisively defeat Napoleon.
congress-of-vienna: The great powers redraw the map of Europe around a balance of power.
waterloo: Napoleon's final defeat; he is exiled to St Helena.
greek-independence: Revolt against Ottoman rule breaks out in the Peloponnese; Greece is independent by 1830.
railway: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens and the railway age begins.
belgium: A revolt in Brussels separates Belgium from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
algeria-1830: French colonial rule in North Africa begins.
revolutions-1848: The February Revolution topples France's July Monarchy, and revolution sweeps across Europe.
communist-manifesto: Marx and Engels publish it in London.
sevastopol: In the Crimean War (1853–1856), Britain, France and the Ottomans besiege the Russian fortress.
solferino: France and Piedmont-Sardinia defeat Austria; the carnage leads to the founding of the Red Cross.
kingdom-of-italy: Victor Emmanuel II is proclaimed King of Italy in Turin.
serfdom: Alexander II's emancipation decree frees the serfs.
koniggratz: Prussia defeats Austria and takes the lead in German unification.
compromise-1867: The Austrian Empire becomes the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary.
suez: The sea route between Europe and Asia becomes much shorter.
sedan: Napoleon III is captured and the Second French Empire collapses.
german-empire: Wilhelm I is proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.
congress-of-berlin: Serbia, Montenegro and Romania become independent; Bulgaria gains autonomy.
berlin-conference: The powers set rules for the partition of Africa (1884–1885).
russia-1905: After Bloody Sunday, the tsar is forced to create the State Duma.
bosnia-annexed: The Bosnian Crisis raises tension in the Balkans.
balkan-war: The Balkan League defeats the Ottomans, who lose nearly all their European territory.
sarajevo: Archduke Franz Ferdinand is shot, setting off the First World War.
marne: France and Britain halt the German advance, and the Western Front settles into trench warfare.
gallipoli: The Allied landings at the Dardanelles fail.
verdun: Nearly ten months of fighting leave more than 700,000 casualties.
october-revolution: The Bolsheviks seize power in Petrograd.
brest-litovsk: Soviet Russia leaves the war and gives up vast western territories.
armistice: The armistice of 11 November ends the First World War.
versailles: Germany loses territory and must pay reparations, and new states are founded.
trianon: Hungary loses about two-thirds of its territory.
march-on-rome: Mussolini takes power and builds a Fascist regime.
ussr-founded: The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics is established.
turkey-republic: Atatürk becomes president, with Ankara as the capital.
hitler: The Nazi Party takes control of Germany.
spanish-civil-war: Franco launches a rebellion; the war lasts until 1939.
munich: Britain and France appease Hitler, and Czechoslovakia must cede the Sudetenland.
invasion-of-poland: The Second World War begins in Europe.
dunkirk: More than 300,000 British and French troops are evacuated; France surrenders soon after.
battle-of-britain: The Royal Air Force withstands the German air offensive.
barbarossa: Germany invades the Soviet Union and the Eastern Front opens.
stalingrad: The turning point on the Eastern Front (1942–1943).
el-alamein: Britain defeats Rommel and the war in North Africa turns.
kursk: One of the largest tank battles in history; Germany loses the initiative in the East.
normandy: The Allies open a Western Front.
yalta: The US, Britain and the Soviet Union plan postwar Europe.
berlin-1945: Soviet forces take Berlin; Germany surrenders unconditionally and the war in Europe ends.
berlin-blockade: The first major crisis of the Cold War (1948–1949).
hungary-1956: The uprising is crushed by Soviet troops.
treaty-of-rome: The European Economic Community is founded.
berlin-wall-built: The symbol of a divided Cold War Europe.
prague-spring: Warsaw Pact troops invade Czechoslovakia and end the reforms.
franco-dies: Spain begins its transition to democracy.
solidarity: A strike at the Gdańsk shipyard creates the first independent trade union in the Eastern Bloc.
chernobyl: One of the worst nuclear power accidents in history.
berlin-wall-falls: Communist rule collapses across Eastern Europe.
ussr-dissolved: Its fifteen republics become independent states.
yugoslav-wars: Slovenia and Croatia declare independence and war follows.
velvet-divorce: The Czech Republic and Slovakia separate peacefully.
euro: The euro launches as an accounting currency and the European Central Bank sets a single monetary policy.
kosovo-war: NATO bombs the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

athens.title: The Century of Athens
athens.lede: From defying Persia to surrendering to Sparta: Athens' most brilliant hundred years.
steps: Persia and Ionia

In the mid-6th century BC the Persian Empire of Cyrus swallowed the Greek cities of the Asia Minor coast. In 499 BC the Ionian cities, led by Miletus, revolted, and Athens sent twenty ships to help. The revolt was crushed after six years and Miletus razed; Darius I resolved to punish Athens for meddling.

p: Miletus, Ephesus and the other Ionian cities on the west coast of Asia Minor grew rich on seaborne trade, and Thales, the first Greek philosopher, was born in Miletus. Persia ruled them through friendly tyrants and took yearly tribute. Under Darius I the empire stretched from the Aegean to the Indus, and he built the Royal Road from Sardis to his capital at Susa.

The spark was a failed expedition. In 500 BC Aristagoras, ruler of Miletus, borrowed Persian forces to attack the island of Naxos; after four months he had failed, and fearing punishment he urged the cities to rise. Sparta refused to help; Athens sent 20 ships and Eretria 5. In 498 BC the rebels took Sardis and burned the lower town. The revolt spread as far as Cyprus, but the Athenians soon went home and Persia retook the cities one by one. In 494 BC the fleets met off the island of Lade near Miletus; the Samians and others deserted mid-battle and the rebels were routed. Miletus fell: most of its men were killed, its women and children enslaved, and the survivors deported to the Persian Gulf.

Herodotus called those 20 ships the beginning of all the troubles between Greeks and Persians. He tells us that when Darius heard of Sardis, he ordered a servant to remind him three times at every dinner not to forget the Athenians. In 492 BC his son-in-law Mardonius marched west along the Thracian coast, but his fleet was wrecked by a storm off Mount Athos and he turned back. The next year Darius sent envoys to demand earth and water, the tokens of submission. Many cities gave them; Athens and Sparta put the envoys to death.

steps: Marathon

In 490 BC a Persian expedition landed at Marathon, north-east of Athens. The outnumbered Athenian hoplites charged and won; by tradition 192 Athenians fell against more than 6,000 Persians. The messenger said to have run back to Athens with the news and died is the origin of the marathon race.

p: In the summer of 490 BC Darius sent a fleet under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean. It first took Eretria, burning its temples and carrying off its people in revenge for Sardis. Hippias, the exiled tyrant of Athens, sailed with them and advised landing at Marathon: a wide bay, a plain fit for cavalry, and about 40 km from Athens. Modern scholars put the Persian force at around 20,000 to 25,000. Athens sent the runner Pheidippides some 240 km to Sparta for help; he arrived the next day, but religious custom forbade the Spartans to march before the full moon.

About 9,000 Athenian hoplites marched to Marathon, joined only by some 1,000 men from little Plataea. The ten generals were divided; Miltiades pressed for battle, and the polemarch Callimachus cast the deciding vote. Miltiades thinned his centre and massed his strength on the wings. With about 1.5 km to cover, the Athenians advanced at a run. The Persian centre broke through, but the victorious Greek wings closed in from both sides and the Persians fled to their ships, seven of which were captured. Callimachus was killed, and so was a brother of the playwright Aeschylus.

The Persian fleet then sailed round Cape Sounion towards Athens, but the army had hurried back, and the Persians sailed home. Two thousand Spartans arrived only after the battle, in time to view the Persian dead. Marathon shattered the belief that the Persian army could not be beaten. The tale of the messenger who ran to Athens and died is not in Herodotus but in much later writers; the first modern Olympic Games, in 1896, created the marathon race in its honour.

steps: Thermopylae and Salamis

Ten years later Xerxes I came in person, by land and sea. King Leonidas of Sparta held the Persian army at Thermopylae for three days and died with his men; the Athenians abandoned their city for their ships. Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow straits of Salamis and smashed it in a day. Xerxes went back to Asia, and the next year his army was beaten at Plataea.

p: Darius died in 486 BC. His son Xerxes I put down a revolt in Egypt and then prepared with great care: he bridged the Hellespont with boats and cut a canal through the Athos peninsula. Herodotus put his army at 1.7 million men; modern scholars estimate between 100,000 and 300,000. In Athens, Themistocles persuaded the Assembly to spend the income from a rich new silver strike at Laurion on about 200 triremes.

In late summer 480 BC about 7,000 Greeks held Thermopylae, a narrow pass between the mountains and the sea. For two days the Persians attacked head-on and failed, until a local man, Ephialtes, led them along a mountain path to the Greek rear. Leonidas sent most of the allies away and stayed behind with his 300 Spartans and some allied troops. The Persians then marched into Attica and burned the Acropolis. In September Themistocles sent word to Xerxes that the Greek fleet was about to slip away by night, and the Persian ships sealed the straits that very night. Next day more than 300 Greek ships met them in the narrows, where the larger Persian fleet had no room to manoeuvre and its ships fouled one another. Xerxes watched the rout from the shore.

Xerxes went home with most of his army, leaving picked troops under Mardonius. In 479 BC the Spartan Pausanias led the allied Greeks to victory at Plataea, where Mardonius was killed. Persia never again invaded mainland Greece. Salamis had been won by the Athenian fleet, rowed mostly by the poorest citizens, and their weight in the city's politics grew accordingly. In 472 BC Aeschylus, who is said to have fought in the battle, staged his tragedy The Persians.

steps: The golden age

After the war the Aegean cities formed the Delian League under Athens, keeping its treasury on Delos. Athens turned its allies into subjects and used their money to rebuild the Acropolis. In the thirty years of Pericles, work began on the Parthenon, the tragedies of Aeschylus and Sophocles were staged and Herodotus wrote his Histories.

p: The Delian League was founded in 478 BC to drive the Persians from the Aegean and free Ionia. Members supplied either ships or money, and the Athenian Aristides set their combined annual contribution at 460 talents. Most of the smaller states preferred to pay, so Athens used their money to enlarge its own fleet while the allies lost the means to defend themselves. Around 470 BC Naxos tried to leave and was besieged into submission. In 454 BC the treasury was moved from Delos to Athens, and the league became, in effect, an Athenian empire.

From 443 BC Pericles was elected general almost every year, and dominated Athenian politics until his death in 429 BC. He introduced pay for jurors so that poorer men could take part in public life, and in 451 BC carried a law limiting citizenship to those with two Athenian parents. In 447 BC work began on the Parthenon, designed by Ictinus and Callicrates, with sculpture directed by Phidias. The main building was finished nine years later; inside stood Phidias's statue of Athena in gold and ivory, about 12 metres tall.

According to Plutarch, critics accused Pericles of using the allies' money to dress Athens up like a vain woman; he replied that so long as Athens kept the Persians away, how it spent the money was its own business. Athens became the cultural capital of the Greek world. Aeschylus's Oresteia trilogy was staged in 458 BC, Sophocles wrote Antigone, Herodotus is said to have given public readings of his work here, and the young Socrates argued in the streets. Thucydides later remarked that Athens was a democracy in name but in practice was ruled by its first citizen.

steps: The Peloponnesian War

Athenian power alarmed Sparta and Corinth, and in 431 BC war broke out. Each year Sparta invaded Attica while the Athenians sheltered behind their walls; in the second year plague swept the crowded city and killed Pericles. In 415 BC Athens staked everything on an expedition against Syracuse in Sicily, and two years later lost it all.

p: Athens meddled in Corinth's quarrel with Corcyra, besieged its rebellious ally Potidaea and barred the Megarians from the harbours of its empire, and Corinth urged Sparta to fight. Thucydides held that the real cause was Sparta's fear of Athens' growing power. At the outbreak Athens had 300 warships and 6,000 talents of silver on the Acropolis. Pericles' plan was to abandon the countryside, bring everyone inside Athens and Piraeus, joined by the Long Walls, live on grain shipped in by sea and avoid battle on land.

In the summer of 430 BC plague broke out in the packed city and returned on and off for several years, killing about a quarter of the population; what it was is still unknown. Thucydides caught it, survived and left a detailed account. Pericles died of it in 429 BC. In 421 BC the two sides made the Peace of Nicias, but it was peace in name only. In 415 BC Alcibiades talked Athens into invading Sicily, and 134 triremes sailed with about 5,000 hoplites. Soon afterwards Alcibiades was recalled to face charges of sacrilege, and he went over to Sparta.

Sparta sent Gylippus to help defend Syracuse. Athens sent 73 more warships but still could not take the city. In 413 BC the Athenian fleet was beaten in the Great Harbour; the army was cut to pieces in its retreat, the generals Nicias and Demosthenes were executed, and more than 7,000 prisoners were penned in the stone quarries, where many died. That same year Sparta planted a permanent garrison at Decelea in Attica, and according to Thucydides more than 20,000 slaves fled from Athens. The allies began to waver, and Persia began to fund Sparta.
facts: about a quarter of the population

steps: Athens surrenders

Sparta built a fleet with Persian money. In 405 BC Lysander caught the Athenian fleet on the beach at Aegospotami in the Hellespont and destroyed it. The next year Athens surrendered and pulled down the Long Walls to its port. Its political supremacy was over, but its philosophy was only beginning: five years later Socrates stood trial in the city.

p: Athens held out for nine more years after Sicily. From 407 BC the Persian prince Cyrus the Younger funded Sparta, so that its fleet could offer higher pay and lure rowers away from Athens. Athens still won at sea, at Cyzicus in 410 BC and at the Arginusae Islands in 406 BC. But after that battle a storm prevented the rescue of men in the water, and the Assembly condemned the victorious generals together; six were executed.

In 405 BC Lysander took the Spartan fleet to Lampsacus on the Hellespont, threatening the Black Sea grain route on which Athens lived. The Athenians arrived with 180 ships and beached them across the strait at Aegospotami. Each day they rowed out to offer battle, and each day Lysander stayed put. On the fifth day, as the crews scattered ashore to find food, he struck. Most ships were taken on the beach; only the general Conon got away, with about nine. According to Plutarch some 3,000 Athenian prisoners were put to death. Sparta then closed in on Athens by land and sea, and famine set in.

In the spring of 404 BC Athens surrendered. Corinth and Thebes wanted the city destroyed; Sparta refused, citing Athens' service against Persia. Athens had to give up its fleet except for 12 ships, recall its exiles and follow Sparta's lead abroad. The Thirty Tyrants installed by Sparta ran a reign of terror and killed about 1,500 people before democracy was restored the next year. In 399 BC Socrates was charged with impiety and corrupting the young, and a jury of about 500 citizens sentenced him to death; he drank hemlock. His pupil Plato would later found the Academy in Athens.

alexander.title: Alexander's Conquests
alexander.lede: In twelve years a king of Macedon marched to the Indus.
steps: The rise of Macedon

To the Greek cities, Macedon in the north was a half-civilised borderland. Philip II rebuilt its army around the long-pike phalanx and heavy cavalry, and in 338 BC beat Athens and Thebes at Chaeronea to become master of Greece. Two years later he was assassinated, and his twenty-year-old son Alexander, once a pupil of Aristotle, became king.

p: Macedon's royal house claimed descent from Argos in Greece, but the cities of the south looked down on this land of kings and nobles. When Philip II came to the throne in 359 BC, Macedon had just been beaten by the Illyrians and its king killed. As a youth Philip had been a hostage in Thebes, where he studied the best army in Greece. He armed his infantry with the sarissa, a pike about 5.5 metres long, and drew them up 16 ranks deep, while the noble Companion cavalry delivered the decisive blow. The gold mines of Mount Pangaion paid for a standing army and for bribes.

In 338 BC Athens and Thebes met the Macedonians at Chaeronea, each side some 30,000 strong. Philip, it is said, feigned a retreat on his right to draw the Athenians forward, while the eighteen-year-old Alexander, commanding the other wing, was the first to break the Sacred Band, Thebes' elite. Ancient writers report 1,000 Athenians killed and 2,000 captured. The next year every Greek state except Sparta joined the League of Corinth under Philip and voted for war on Persia; an advance force crossed into Asia Minor in the spring of 336 BC.

Later that year, at his daughter's wedding in the old capital of Aegae, Philip was stabbed to death at the theatre entrance by Pausanias, one of his own bodyguards. He was 46. The motive is still debated, and some suspected Alexander's mother Olympias, or even Alexander himself. From the age of 13 Alexander had been taught by Aristotle for about three years. When Thebes rebelled the next year he razed the city, sparing only the temples and the house of the poet Pindar.

steps: Across the sea

In the spring of 334 BC Alexander crossed the Hellespont with nearly 40,000 men. At the river Granicus he led the cavalry across himself and routed the army of the Persian satraps; the Greek cities of the Asia Minor coast went over to him one after another.

p: Alexander left Macedon in the hands of the veteran Antipater, with about 12,000 infantry and 1,500 cavalry to hold Greece. He took about 32,000 infantry and 5,000 cavalry: the Macedonian phalanx and the Companions, Greek allies and light troops. According to Plutarch the treasury held only 70 talents when he set out, against debts of 200. On the way he visited Troy and sacrificed at the tomb of Achilles, casting the expedition as a new Trojan War.

On the Persian side, the satraps met in council at Zelea. Memnon, a Greek mercenary general in Darius's service, urged them to burn the land and avoid battle; unwilling to burn their own provinces, they chose to fight at the Granicus. In May 334 BC the Persian cavalry lined the steep eastern bank, with the Greek mercenary infantry behind. Alexander led the Companions across the river himself. In the melee his helmet was split, and a Persian noble was about to strike him from behind when Cleitus the Black cut off the man's arm. Once the Persian cavalry broke, the abandoned Greek mercenaries were surrounded and almost wiped out; about 2,000 were captured and sent to Macedon for hard labour.

Arrian puts the Macedonian dead at little more than a hundred, probably too low. Alexander sent 300 sets of Persian armour to Athens as an offering to Athena, dedicated by 'the Greeks except the Spartans', presenting the campaign as all Greece's revenge. Sardis then surrendered, and Ephesus and other cities expelled their pro-Persian oligarchs and set up democracies. He also disbanded his fleet, which was no match for the Persian navy, and resolved to break Persian sea power from the land by seizing its harbours.

steps: Issus

In 333 BC Darius III met him at Issus with a great army. Alexander's cavalry drove straight for the Great King in the centre, and Darius fled, leaving his mother, wife and daughters as captives. Rather than pursue him, Alexander marched down the coast and spent seven months taking Tyre, the base of the Persian fleet.

p: In the spring of 333 BC Alexander reached Gordium in Phrygia, where legend said that whoever undid the tangled knot there would rule Asia; he reportedly cut it with his sword. That year Memnon, leading a Persian counter-attack in the Aegean, died of illness, easing the pressure on Alexander. Darius III gathered a great army at Babylon. Ancient writers put it at 600,000; most modern scholars estimate fewer than 100,000. Alexander was delayed by illness at Tarsus, and Darius later slipped round behind him, cutting his line of retreat.

In November the armies met across the river Pinarus, on a narrow coastal plain by the Gulf of Issus, between mountains and sea, where Persian numbers counted for little. Alexander took his usual place on the right; the Companions broke the Persian left, then wheeled towards the centre and made straight for Darius's chariot. The Great King turned and fled, and his army collapsed behind him. Alexander treated the captured queen mother, queen and princesses with royal honour. Parmenion also seized much of the Persian royal treasure at Damascus.

Tyre, on an island less than a kilometre offshore, thought its high walls impregnable. Alexander set his men to build a causeway out into the sea, but the Tyrians burned his siege towers with a fireship. The turn came at sea: seeing that Persia's cause was lost, the kings of the Phoenician cities and of Cyprus came over to Alexander with about 200 warships. The city fell in the summer of 332 BC; according to Arrian about 8,000 were killed and 30,000 sold into slavery. During the siege Darius wrote offering a ransom of 10,000 talents and all the land west of the Euphrates. Alexander refused.

steps: Egypt and Gaugamela

Egypt surrendered without a fight, and Alexander founded Alexandria on the coast west of the Nile delta. In 331 BC he crossed the Euphrates and the Tigris and beat Darius again at Gaugamela. Babylon, Susa and Persepolis opened their gates; Darius was murdered by his own men as he fled, and the Achaemenid Empire was finished.

p: After Tyre, Alexander spent two more months taking Gaza. At the end of 332 BC he entered Egypt, where Persian rule was hated, and the satrap opened the gates. The Egyptians accepted him as pharaoh. He crossed the Libyan desert to the oracle of Ammon at the oasis of Siwa, where the priest hailed him as son of Ammon. The site of the new city lay on the western edge of the Nile delta, between Lake Mareotis and the sea, and was laid out by the architect Dinocrates. It later became the capital of the Ptolemies, famous for its Library and the Pharos lighthouse.

On 1 October 331 BC the armies met on the plain of Gaugamela, east of the Tigris. Darius had chosen flat, open ground and had it levelled so that his 200 scythed chariots could charge. Ancient writers credited him with a million men; modern estimates run from 50,000 to 100,000. Alexander had about 47,000. He moved his whole line obliquely to the right, drawing the Persian left-wing cavalry after him until a gap opened in the Persian centre. Alexander led the Companions in a wedge straight through it towards Darius, and Darius fled again.

The satrap of Babylon surrendered the city. At Susa Alexander took about 50,000 talents of silver, and in 330 BC the palace at Persepolis went up in flames, for reasons still debated. Darius fled east, and in the summer of 330 BC he was seized and killed by Bessus, satrap of Bactria, and others. Alexander gave the body a royal burial and presented himself as heir to the Achaemenids. He was no longer just the avenger of the Greeks; he meant to be king of Asia.

steps: Death in Babylon

Alexander pushed on east over the Hindu Kush to the Indus valley, until his soldiers refused to go further. In 323 BC, back in Babylon and planning an invasion of Arabia, he fell ill with fever and died ten days later at 32. Asked on his deathbed who should have the empire, he is said to have answered: 'The strongest.'

p: From 329 to 327 BC Alexander fought a gruelling campaign in Bactria and Sogdiana, today's northern Afghanistan and southern Central Asia, against elusive guerrilla bands, and in the end married Roxana, daughter of a local noble. He took on more and more of the dress and ceremony of the Persian court, and the gulf between him and his Macedonian veterans widened. In 330 BC Parmenion was put to death, and in 328 BC, in a drunken quarrel, Alexander killed with his own hand Cleitus, the man who had saved his life at the Granicus.

In 327 BC he crossed the Hindu Kush again and entered India. In 326 BC he defeated King Porus and his war elephants at the Hydaspes (the modern Jhelum), then left Porus to rule his kingdom. His horse Bucephalus died that year, and he founded a city named after it. Further east, at the Hyphasis (the modern Beas), soldiers eight years from home refused to go on. After shutting himself in his tent for three days, Alexander gave the order to turn back. On the way home he led part of the army through the Gedrosian desert, with terrible losses.

Back at Susa in 324 BC he held a mass wedding at which some 80 of his officers married Persian noblewomen, while he took a daughter of Darius. In June 323 BC he died in Babylon. The cause is still unknown: malaria, typhoid fever and poison have all been suggested. He left no adult heir. His son, Alexander IV, was born months later, and his half-brother Arrhidaeus was mentally impaired. The generals made the two joint kings, with Perdiccas as regent, but kept real power for themselves.

steps: The successors

His generals fought over the inheritance for more than forty years. In 301 BC an alliance of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander defeated and killed the strongest of them, Antigonus I, at Ipsus, and the break-up became permanent: Ptolemy held Egypt, Seleucus Asia, and Macedon itself became a separate kingdom. Greek language and Greek cities now spread from the Nile to Central Asia.

p: The joint kingship soon became a fiction. Ptolemy made Egypt his own, even hijacking Alexander's body and burying it there. The regent Perdiccas invaded Egypt, failed, and was murdered by his own officers. After that the most powerful of the generals was Antigonus the One-Eyed, who with his son Demetrius, 'the Besieger', for a time controlled most of Asia. Alexander's mother, widow and son were all murdered in turn. From 306 BC Antigonus and Demetrius took the title of king, and the other generals soon followed.

In 301 BC the two sides met at Ipsus in Phrygia, in central Asia Minor. Antigonus, now about 80, and Demetrius faced Lysimachus, Seleucus and troops sent by Cassander; each army is said to have numbered 70,000 to 80,000. Seleucus brought about 400 war elephants: he had ceded his eastern lands to Chandragupta of the Indian Maurya Empire in return for a great herd of them. Demetrius routed the enemy horse but pursued too far, and on his way back found the elephants blocking his path; Antigonus's infantry was left exposed, and the old king was killed by javelins. Demetrius escaped and later, for a time, became king of Macedon.

The victors divided Antigonus's lands, and over the following decades three main kingdoms took shape: the Ptolemies ruled Egypt until Cleopatra's death in 30 BC; the Seleucids held Syria, Mesopotamia and Iran; and from 276 BC Macedon was held by Antigonus's grandson Antigonus II and his heirs. The nearly three centuries after Alexander are known as the Hellenistic Age. A common Greek was spoken from the Mediterranean to Central Asia, and at Ai Khanoum in northern Afghanistan archaeologists have uncovered a Greek city complete with theatre and gymnasium.

rise-of-rome.title: The Rise of Rome
rise-of-rome.lede: How a city of Italy became master of the Mediterranean in little more than two centuries.
steps: The struggle for Sicily

By the early 3rd century BC Rome had united the Italian peninsula. Across the strait, western Sicily belonged to Carthage in North Africa, a trading empire that controlled the sea lanes of the western Mediterranean. In 264 BC the two went to war over Messina. Rome, which had never fought at sea, copied a stranded Carthaginian warship to build a fleet, and twenty-three years later won the war and Sicily.

p: Rome had spent more than two centuries bringing Italy under its control through war and alliance; with the surrender of the Greek city of Tarentum in 272 BC the task was all but complete. Carthage, founded by Phoenicians from Tyre in what is now Tunisia, dominated the western Mediterranean through trade and a powerful navy, holding western Sicily, Sardinia and footholds on the Spanish coast. Messina had been seized by Italian mercenaries calling themselves Mamertines; threatened by King Hiero II of Syracuse, they appealed to both Carthage and Rome. Rome chose to intervene.

The Roman army soon gained a foothold in Sicily, and in 263 BC Hiero II changed sides. But without a navy Rome could not cut Carthage's supply lines. Around 261 BC Rome built 100 quinqueremes and 20 triremes. To make up for their lack of seamanship the Romans fitted their bows with the corvus, or 'raven', a boarding bridge with an iron spike that gripped an enemy ship so that soldiers could storm across, turning a sea battle into a land battle. With it the consul Duilius won Rome's first naval victory at Mylae in 260 BC.

The war dragged on longer than expected. In 256 BC a Roman army landed in Africa, only to be defeated the following year and its commander Regulus captured; Roman fleets were nearly destroyed by storms more than once. By Polybius's count Rome lost about 700 warships and Carthage about 500. In 241 BC a new fleet, paid for by wealthy citizens, won a decisive victory off the Aegates Islands, and Carthage sued for peace: it left Sicily and agreed to pay 3,200 talents within ten years. Sicily became Rome's first overseas province.

steps: Hannibal

In 218 BC the Carthaginian general Hannibal set out from Spain with infantry, cavalry and dozens of elephants, crossed the Alps and appeared in northern Italy. In 216 BC at Cannae he enveloped a Roman army of about 80,000; ancient writers put the Roman dead at more than 50,000. But most of Rome's Italian allies stayed loyal, Rome refused to make peace, and Hannibal fought on in Italy for fifteen years without ever attacking Rome itself.

p: After the First Punic War the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca turned to Spain, opening mines and training troops; his son-in-law Hasdrubal founded New Carthage, modern Cartagena. In 221 BC Hannibal, then about 25, took command of the army in Spain. In 219 BC he besieged Rome's ally Saguntum and took it after eight months, and Rome declared war.

In the spring of 218 BC Hannibal marched north, crossed the Pyrenees and the Rhône, and in late autumn went over the Alps, battered by cold, snow and attacks from mountain tribes. According to Polybius he reached Italy with only about 20,000 infantry and 6,000 cavalry, and most of his 37 elephants did not survive the first winter. He won at the Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. In August 216 BC at Cannae he drew up a line thin in the centre and strong on the wings. His centre gave ground, the African infantry on the wings closed in, and his cavalry fell on the Roman rear until the Romans were trapped. Ancient accounts of the Roman dead range from nearly 50,000 to 70,000, among them the consul Paullus; Hannibal lost some 6,000 to 8,000.

After Cannae, Capua and other cities of southern Italy, and Syracuse in Sicily, went over to Carthage, and Philip V of Macedon allied himself with Hannibal. But the Latin colonies and most of the allies stayed loyal. Rome refused to ransom its prisoners, raised new legions and returned to the strategy of Fabius 'the Delayer': avoid pitched battle and wear the enemy down. In 211 BC Hannibal marched to the walls of Rome, but only to draw the Romans away from their siege of Capua; he never actually assaulted the city.

steps: Zama

Rome struck at Carthage's bases instead. Scipio took Spain, then landed in Africa. In 202 BC Hannibal, recalled home, was beaten at Zama; Carthage gave up its fleet and Spain and became a minor power. On the map Rome now holds eastern and southern Spain.

p: In 211 BC Scipio's father and uncle were defeated and killed in Spain. The next year the younger Scipio, then only about 25, volunteered to take over the war there. In 209 BC his men waded across a shallow lagoon and took New Carthage, Carthage's headquarters in Spain, in a single day. In 207 BC Hannibal's brother Hasdrubal crossed the Alps with reinforcements, but his army was destroyed at the Metaurus river in Italy, and his head was thrown into Hannibal's camp. In 206 BC Scipio won at Ilipa and drove the Carthaginians out of Spain for good.

Elected consul for 205 BC, Scipio landed in Africa the next year, allied himself with the Numidian prince Masinissa and beat the Carthaginians twice in 203 BC. Carthage hastily recalled Hannibal. In the autumn of 202 BC the armies met near Zama. Hannibal had about 40,000 men and 80 elephants; Scipio had somewhat fewer, but Masinissa's Numidian cavalry fought on his side. Scipio left lanes in his line so that the panicking elephants passed through; the Roman and Numidian horse chased off the Carthaginian cavalry, then returned to strike Hannibal's infantry from behind. According to Polybius about 20,000 Carthaginians were killed, against some 1,500 Romans.

The peace of 201 BC was harsh. Carthage gave up Spain and all its overseas possessions, handed over all its elephants, kept only 10 warships, agreed to pay 10,000 talents over 50 years, and could make no war without Rome's consent. Scipio earned the name Africanus. In 197 BC Rome set up two provinces in Spain, Nearer and Further. A few years later Hannibal was forced into exile and took refuge with the Seleucid king Antiochus III.

steps: Conquering the East

Rome then turned to the Hellenistic world. In 168 BC the legions broke the Macedonian phalanx at Pydna, and twenty years later Macedon became a Roman province. In 146 BC Rome razed both Carthage and Corinth in the same year, and Carthage's homeland became the province of Africa. No state around the Mediterranean could now stand up to Rome.

p: Less than two years after Zama, Rome was at war again with Philip V of Macedon; it defeated him at Cynoscephalae in 197 BC. In 190 BC Rome crushed the Seleucid king Antiochus III at Magnesia in Asia Minor. Philip's son Perseus rebuilt Macedon's strength, and in 171 BC the Third Macedonian War broke out.

On 22 June 168 BC the consul Aemilius Paullus met Perseus at Pydna. Head-on, the phalanx was irresistible, but as it advanced over broken ground gaps opened in its ranks. The legionaries worked their way into them in small units, and at close quarters the pikemen were helpless. Ancient writers report over 20,000 Macedonians killed and only about 100 Romans. Perseus was captured and paraded in Paullus's triumph. Macedon was first split into four republics, then, after a revolt was put down in 148 BC, made a province.

Carthage's trade revived, and by 151 BC it had paid off its indemnity; Cato the Elder is said to have called for its destruction every time he spoke in the Senate. In 149 BC Rome declared war on the pretext that Carthage had broken the treaty by fighting Masinissa, and ordered its people to abandon the city and move about 15 km inland. They refused and held out for nearly three years. In the spring of 146 BC Scipio Aemilianus broke in; after six days of street fighting the roughly 50,000 survivors were sold into slavery and the city was burned. That same year the general Mummius crushed the Achaean League in Greece, sacked Corinth and shipped its art to Rome. The story that the Romans sowed the ruins of Carthage with salt has no basis in ancient sources.

steps: Caesar

Conquest brought wealth, and civil war: armies now answered to their generals. From 58 to 50 BC Caesar conquered all of Gaul, defeating Vercingetorix at the siege of Alesia in 52 BC. When the Senate ordered him to give up his command, he led his army across the Rubicon in 49 BC, won the civil war and became dictator for life.

p: Conquest made the senatorial elite and businessmen immensely rich, while slave-worked estates ruined many small farmers. From 107 BC Marius enlisted landless poor men, who looked to their commander to win them land on discharge, and armies became the personal forces of their generals. In 88 BC Sulla became the first to march his army into Rome. In 60 BC Caesar, Pompey and Crassus formed a private pact known as the First Triumvirate, and Caesar went on to govern Gaul and neighbouring provinces with four legions.

Caesar defeated the Helvetii, Ariovistus's Germans and the Belgae, and twice landed in Britain. In 52 BC Vercingetorix, chief of the Arverni, united the Gallic tribes in a great revolt, then fell back to the hill town of Alesia. Caesar ringed it with two lines of fortifications: an inner line about 16 km long to pen in the defenders, and an outer one about 21 km long to hold off the Gallic relief army. Caesar claimed the relief force was 250,000 strong, a figure modern scholars think greatly exaggerated. The Romans beat off the relief army, and Vercingetorix surrendered. Six years later he was paraded in Caesar's triumph and then executed.

Plutarch says a million people were killed in the Gallic Wars and another million enslaved; these are ancient estimates. In January 49 BC Caesar crossed the Rubicon, the boundary between his province and Italy, with a single legion, and Pompey and most of the Senate fled to Greece. In 48 BC Caesar crushed Pompey at Pharsalus; Pompey was murdered in Egypt. Caesar's Julian calendar, in force from 1 January 45 BC, with 365 days and a leap year every four years, was used for more than 1,600 years.
facts: inner about 16 km, outer about 21 km

steps: From republic to empire

On the Ides of March, 44 BC, Caesar was stabbed to death in the Senate. His adopted son Octavian and Mark Antony first shared power, then fell out; in 31 BC Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, at Actium and annexed Egypt the next year. In 27 BC the Senate named him Augustus. The forms of the Republic survived, but power now lay with one man. By the turn of the era Rome ringed the whole Mediterranean.

p: More than sixty men took part in the murder, led by Brutus and Cassius. They believed that killing a 'tyrant' would restore the Republic, but popular fury drove them from Rome. In his will Caesar adopted his eighteen-year-old great-nephew Octavian. In 43 BC Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate and purged their enemies; Cicero was among those killed. In 42 BC Octavian and Antony defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. Octavian then took the West and Antony the East, where he became the ally and partner of Cleopatra, queen of Egypt.

Relations between the two broke down, and at Octavian's urging the Senate declared war on Cleopatra. On 2 September 31 BC the fleets met off the promontory of Actium on the west coast of Greece, Octavian's under the command of Agrippa. Cleopatra broke out with 60 ships and fled south; Antony followed, and the fleet and army he left behind soon surrendered. In August 30 BC Octavian entered Alexandria; Antony and Cleopatra took their own lives and the Ptolemaic dynasty came to an end. Egypt, run by a governor Octavian chose himself, became Rome's granary.

In January 27 BC Octavian announced that he was restoring the Republic. The Senate granted him the name Augustus, 'the revered one', and left him in charge of the provinces where most of the legions were stationed. He called himself princeps, 'first citizen'; the Senate and assemblies carried on as before, but the army, money and appointments were in his hands. He ruled until his death in AD 14. By his own record, the census of 8 BC counted 4,233,000 Roman citizens. The two centuries or so that followed are known as the Pax Romana.

fall-of-rome.title: The Fall of the West
fall-of-rome.lede: In a century the western half of the empire became a set of Germanic kingdoms.
steps: Adrianople

In 376 Goths driven west by the Huns asked to cross the Danube and shelter in the empire. Roman officials starved and abused the refugees, and the Goths rose in revolt. In 378 the eastern emperor Valens gave battle at Adrianople; the Roman army was destroyed and the emperor killed. From then on the Goths remained inside the empire as a people under arms.

p: In the 370s the Huns burst out of the Central Asian steppe, crushing the Alans and then the Gothic kingdom north of the Black Sea. Another Gothic group on the Danube, led by Fritigern, gathered on the bank and asked to be let in. Valens, at war with Persia and short of soldiers, agreed, meaning them to farm and fight for the empire. No reliable figure survives for how many crossed; modern estimates run to tens of thousands, far more than frontier officials could handle.

Roman commanders such as Lupicinus profiteered from the shortage; the historian Ammianus Marcellinus says starving Goths traded their children for dog meat. Lupicinus then tried to murder the Gothic leaders at a banquet in Marcianople. Fritigern escaped and went to war, plundering Thrace. In summer 378 Valens hurried back from Antioch, while his nephew Gratian, the western emperor, marched east to help. Told the Goths numbered only about 10,000, Valens attacked on 9 August without waiting. After hours of marching in blazing heat, his men went at the Gothic wagon circle just as the Gothic cavalry returned and struck their flank. The Roman left collapsed and the infantry were packed so tight they could barely use their weapons.

Modern estimates put the Roman army at 15,000 to 30,000 men; Ammianus says about two-thirds died, among them two senior generals and dozens of high officers. Valens's body was never found. Ammianus likened the disaster to Cannae, Rome's great defeat by Hannibal. The best of the eastern field army was gone in a day, and the empire could no longer drive the Goths out; it had to negotiate. In January 379 Gratian made Theodosius, a general from Spain, emperor in the East.

steps: East and West

Theodosius I made peace with the Goths and settled them in the Balkans as 'federates'; in 380 he made Nicene Christianity the state religion. When he died in 395 his two young sons ruled the East and the West. The empire was never reunited: the East was rich and well fortified, while the West came to depend more and more on Germanic generals and their followers.

p: Theodosius spent several years fighting and bargaining with the Goths. A treaty of 382 let them settle south of the Danube under their own leaders, fighting for the empire in war as 'federates'. In effect Rome accepted a self-governing armed people within its borders. In religion, his Edict of Thessalonica of 380 required his subjects to hold the Nicene creed; the Council of Constantinople in 381 condemned Arianism as heresy, and pagan sacrifice was later banned.

In 394 Theodosius defeated the western usurper Eugenius at the River Frigidus. His Gothic federates led the attack and suffered heavy losses; among them was the young Alaric. In January 395 Theodosius died in Milan. Arcadius, about 17, ruled from Constantinople, and Honorius, aged 10, in the West, where real power lay with the half-Vandal general Stilicho. The two courts soon distrusted each other, and Alaric rose with the Goths and played one against the other.

By 400 the two halves were on different paths. The East drew the taxes of Egypt, Syria and Asia Minor, and Constantinople, with water on three sides, was hard to take. That very year the eastern court threw out its overbearing Gothic general Gainas, and many Goths in the city were massacred. The West had the long Rhine frontier to hold on far smaller revenues and handed its defence more and more to Germanic generals like Stilicho. The East also used gold and titles to steer trouble westward, and that gap shaped the two halves' very different fates.

steps: Rome falls

The Visigothic leader Alaric demanded land and office from the western court, and three times marched on Rome. In August 410 he took the city and sacked it for three days. It was the first time in nearly 800 years that Rome had fallen to an enemy, and the news shook the Mediterranean world; Augustine wrote The City of God in response. Around the same years Roman rule in Britain came to an end.

p: After rising in 395, Alaric spent years on the move; when he invaded Italy in 402, Stilicho drove him back at Pollentia and elsewhere. The West had worse troubles. On the last day of 406, by the traditional date, Vandals, Alans and Sueves crossed the Rhine into Gaul, and the army in Britain proclaimed its own emperor, Constantine III, who in 407 took most of its troops across to Gaul. In 408 Honorius had Stilicho executed for treason; the families of Germanic soldiers were massacred, and many of the soldiers went over to Alaric.

Without Stilicho, the western court sat behind the marshes of Ravenna and refused to deal, so Alaric besieged Rome instead. In 408 the city raised a ransom of about 5,000 pounds of gold and 30,000 pounds of silver; in 409 he set up a puppet emperor to pressure Ravenna, in vain. On 24 August 410 the Goths entered through the Salarian Gate. Much wealth was carried off, but the churches of St Peter and St Paul served as sanctuaries and most inhabitants survived. Honorius's half-sister Galla Placidia was taken captive.

The last enemy to enter Rome had been the Gauls, around 390 BC. In Bethlehem, Jerome wrote as if the whole world had fallen with the city; pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods. Augustine began The City of God in 413 as his answer and worked on it for more than a decade. Alaric meant to cross to North Africa, but storms wrecked his fleet and he died in southern Italy that same year. As for Britain, its garrison had already gone; Honorius reportedly wrote to its cities in 410 telling them to see to their own defence.

steps: Huns and Vandals

The Vandals crossed from Spain and in 439 took Carthage, the West's most important source of grain and taxes. Attila's Hunnic empire extorted tribute from both East and West from its base on the Danube plain, and in 451 invaded Gaul, where the Roman general Aetius and the Visigoths stopped it on the Catalaunian Plains. Attila died two years later and his empire fell apart.

p: The Vandals crossed the Rhine in 406 and entered Spain in 409. In 429 their king Gaiseric took his whole people across the Strait of Gibraltar, reportedly about 80,000 including women and children. In 430, while they besieged Hippo, its bishop Augustine died there. In October 439 Gaiseric broke the peace and seized Carthage by surprise. North Africa's grain and taxes had fed Rome and paid the western army; now the Vandals built a fleet and raided Sicily and the Italian coast.

The Huns had settled on the Pannonian plain. Attila ruled with his elder brother Bleda from 434 and alone from about 445, ravaging the Balkans until, after 447, the East paid about 6,000 pounds of gold in arrears and 2,100 pounds a year. In 451 he turned west, crossed the Rhine, took Metz and besieged Orléans. Aetius pieced together a coalition: Theodoric I, king of the Visigoths, led his army in person, joined by Alans, Franks and Burgundians. Around late June the armies met in what is now north-eastern France. Theodoric fell, and Attila withdrew behind his wagons and then retreated.

No reliable figures survive for either army; the 165,000 dead claimed by one ancient historian are plainly inflated. Attila was far from finished: in 452 he invaded Italy and destroyed Aquileia, turning back after meeting envoys who included Pope Leo I. In 453 he died suddenly on his wedding night. His sons fought over the succession, and about a year later subject peoples led by the Gepids routed the Huns at the River Nedao. Yet the West had little left: Africa was lost, much of Gaul and Spain was in other hands, and in 454 Valentinian III killed Aetius with his own hand.

steps: By now the western emperors were puppets of their generals. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, declaring that the West needed no emperor of its own. Contemporaries may not have seen it as the end of an era, but later historians made this year the end of the Western Empire and the start of the Middle Ages.

p: In 455 Valentinian III was murdered by former followers of Aetius, and the male line of Theodosius came to an end. That same year the Vandals came by sea and sacked Rome for two weeks. Between 455 and 476 the West had nine emperors, while real power lay with Ricimer, a general of Suevic descent who made and unmade several of them. In 468 East and West together sent a fleet said to number over a thousand ships against North Africa; off Cape Bon the Vandals destroyed it with fireships, and with it the last hope of recovering Carthage.

In 475 the general Orestes drove out the emperor Julius Nepos and put his own young son Romulus on the throne, mocked as 'Augustulus', the little Augustus. The Germanic soldiers in Italy demanded a third of the land; when Orestes refused, they chose Odoacer, said to be a Scirian, as their leader. In August 476 Odoacer killed Orestes at Piacenza, and on 4 September he entered Ravenna and deposed Romulus, but spared his life and sent him with a pension to an estate near Naples.

Through the Roman Senate, Odoacer told the eastern emperor Zeno that one emperor was enough and that he asked only to govern Italy as an imperial official. Zeno replied evasively, reminding them that the West still had a lawful emperor in Nepos, who lived on in Dalmatia until 480. The Senate still met and the law and administration carried on, so few felt that the sky had fallen. Only in the early 6th century did the eastern chronicler Marcellinus Comes state plainly that the Roman Empire of the West had perished with this Augustulus.

steps: New kingdoms

By about 500 the West had become a handful of Germanic kingdoms. The Ostrogoth Theodoric ruled Italy from Ravenna, the Visigoths held Spain, the Vandals North Africa, and the Frankish king Clovis had united most of Gaul and been baptised a Catholic at Reims. Roman law, cities and the Church lived on inside these kingdoms.

p: Odoacer ruled Italy for more than a decade, but relations with the East soured. In 488 Zeno sent Theodoric, leader of the Ostrogoths who had been troubling the Balkans, to overthrow him, ridding himself of a threat without risking an army of his own. As a boy Theodoric had spent years as a hostage in Constantinople and knew Roman ways well. He led his people over the Alps and won battle after battle; after besieging Ravenna for more than two years he made peace with Odoacer in 493, then killed him with his own hands at a banquet.

Theodoric ruled Italy until his death in 526. The Goths served as soldiers while Romans kept their offices and farms; the Senate still met, and Roman aristocrats such as Cassiodorus and Boethius served him. In 500 he visited Rome, addressed the Senate and people, and paid to repair the walls and palace. The Visigoths, ruling from Toulouse, held south-western Gaul and most of Spain; the Burgundians held the Rhône valley; the Vandals still had North Africa. Most of these rulers were Arian Christians, regarded as heretics, and divided by faith from their Catholic Roman subjects.

Clovis was the exception. King of the Salian Franks in his teens, he defeated Syagrius, the last Roman commander in Gaul, at Soissons in 486, and married the Catholic Burgundian princess Clotilde. Bishop Remigius baptised him at Reims, traditionally at Christmas 496, though some scholars put it as late as about 508. Sharing his faith, the bishops and Roman nobles of Gaul backed him. In 507 he beat the Visigoths at Vouillé and took most of south-western Gaul, and the Frankish kingdom became the most lasting successor state in the West.

charlemagne.title: Charlemagne
charlemagne.lede: The Franks rebuilt an empire in the West, then divided it in three two generations later.
steps: Tours

In the early 8th century Arab armies conquered Visigothic Spain within a few years and crossed the Pyrenees into Gaul. In 732 the Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel met them between Tours and Poitiers; the Arab commander was killed and his army withdrew. The Frankish kings by now reigned in name only; real power lay with mayors like Charles.

p: In 711 the Berber commander Tariq crossed the Strait of Gibraltar and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic by the River Guadalete; within a few years the Visigothic kingdom had collapsed. Muslim forces then crossed the Pyrenees, took Narbonne and raided southern Gaul. In 721 Duke Odo of Aquitaine beat off an attack at Toulouse, but in 732 Abd al-Rahman, governor of al-Andalus, routed Odo on the Garonne, sacked Bordeaux and marched north towards the rich abbey of St Martin at Tours.

Desperate, Odo appealed to his old rival Charles Martel, who brought a Frankish army, mostly on foot, and blocked the invaders north of Poitiers. No reliable figures survive for either side; the hundreds of thousands in medieval chronicles are wildly inflated. A Spanish chronicle of 754 describes the Franks standing shoulder to shoulder, motionless as a wall of ice, while the Arab horsemen charged again and again without breaking through. Abd al-Rahman was killed in the fighting, and that night his army slipped away, leaving its tents behind. The battle is traditionally dated to October 732, though some historians argue for 733.

Later writers hailed it as the battle that saved Christian Europe. Historians today are more cautious, seeing it as the defeat of a great raid rather than an invasion; the Arabs held Narbonne until 759. For Charles, though, it mattered greatly: he used it to push his power into Burgundy and Provence, and the nickname Martel, 'the Hammer', later stuck. When the Merovingian king died in 737 he did not bother to name another, ruling the whole realm as mayor of the palace until his own death in 741.

steps: Pepin becomes king

In 751 Charles Martel's son Pepin, with the pope's blessing, deposed the last Merovingian king and took the crown himself, founding the Carolingian dynasty. In return he invaded Italy, beat the Lombards and gave the pope the lands he took around Ravenna: the origin of the Papal States, which would last for more than a thousand years.

p: When Charles Martel died in 741 his sons Carloman and Pepin shared the realm, and for appearances' sake in 743 they found a Merovingian prince to make king.
