In 747 Carloman became a monk, leaving Pepin in sole control. Yet a mayor who took the crown would look like a usurper. So Pepin sent the bishop of Würzburg and the abbot of Saint-Denis to ask Pope Zacharias who should be king, the man with the power or the man with the title. According to the Royal Frankish Annals, the pope replied that it was better for the one who held real power to be called king.

Around November 751 the Frankish nobles chose Pepin as king at Soissons and bishops anointed him, the first time a Frankish king had been anointed like the kings of the Old Testament. Childeric III, the last Merovingian, had his long royal hair shorn and was sent to a monastery. In 754, under pressure from the Lombards, Pope Stephen II crossed the Alps in person; at Saint-Denis he anointed Pepin and his two sons again and named Pepin Patrician of the Romans, making him Rome's protector.

The Lombard king Aistulf had taken Ravenna in 751, ending Byzantine rule in northern Italy, and was now threatening Rome. Pepin invaded Italy in 754 and again in 756, forced Aistulf to hand over Ravenna and the cities around it, and had their keys laid on the tomb of St Peter as a gift to the pope: the Donation of Pepin. So the Papal States were born, lasting until Rome joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1870. This alliance between the Frankish crown and the papacy set the stage for a coronation half a century later.

steps: Roncevaux

Pepin's son Charles, Charlemagne, became king in 768 and went to war almost every year after: he conquered the Lombard kingdom, fought the Saxons for more than thirty years and forced them to convert, and destroyed the Avar khaganate on the Danube. Returning from a campaign in Spain in 778, his rearguard was ambushed by Basques in the Pyrenees, an event that grew into the Song of Roland.

p: Pepin died in 768, and Charles shared the kingdom with his brother Carloman until Carloman's death three years later. In 774, after a nine-month siege of Pavia, he forced the Lombard king Desiderius to surrender and took the title King of the Lombards. The Saxon wars lasted from 772 to 804: Charles destroyed the Saxons' sacred pillar, the Irminsul, and in 782 at Verden reportedly had 4,500 rebels executed. Bavaria was annexed in 788, and campaigns against the Avars in the 790s carried off the treasure they had hoarded for generations.

The Spanish campaign of 778 grew out of feuding in al-Andalus. Muslim governors, among them the governor of Barcelona, opposed the Umayyad emir of Córdoba and asked Charles for help, promising him Zaragoza and other cities. Charles crossed the Pyrenees in two columns, but Zaragoza shut its gates, the siege failed, and the Saxons rose behind him. He turned back, pulling down the walls of Basque Pamplona on the way. On 15 August, as the army threaded the pass of Roncevaux, Basques hidden on the wooded heights fell on the rearguard and baggage train and killed them to a man.

Charlemagne's biographer Einhard names among the dead the royal steward Eggihard, the count of the palace Anselm, and Roland, prefect of the Breton March. More than three centuries later the defeat became the Old French epic the Song of Roland, in which the Basques turn into Saracens and Roland into Charlemagne's nephew and a martyred hero. Charlemagne gave up grand ventures deep into Spain and instead built a buffer zone south of the Pyrenees, taking Barcelona in 801, the core of what became the Spanish March.

steps: Emperor of the Romans

On Christmas Day 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne in St Peter's in Rome. For the first time in more than three centuries the West had an emperor, and his empire ran from the Elbe to the Pyrenees and from the North Sea to beyond Rome. At Aachen Charlemagne gathered scholars who copied the classics, in what is now called the Carolingian Renaissance.

p: In April 799 enemies in Rome attacked Pope Leo III during a procession and tried to put out his eyes and cut out his tongue. Leo fled to Charlemagne at Paderborn in Saxony. In November 800 Charlemagne came to Rome to examine the charges against the pope, and on 23 December Leo publicly swore an oath to clear himself. Two days later, at Christmas Mass, as Charlemagne rose from prayer at the tomb of St Peter, Leo set a crown on his head, and the Romans present acclaimed him emperor.

Einhard says Charlemagne later declared that had he known what the pope intended, he would not have entered the church that day. Perhaps this was modesty; perhaps he disliked seeming to owe his title to the pope. Constantinople found it harder still to accept. Byzantium was then ruled by the Empress Irene alone, so Westerners could argue that the imperial throne was vacant, while the Byzantines saw Charlemagne as a usurper. The dispute dragged on until 812, when Byzantium recognised him as emperor, though not as emperor 'of the Romans'.

In his later years Charlemagne lived mostly at Aachen, where he built his palace chapel. He sent royal envoys, the missi, out in pairs to inspect the provinces, and reformed the coinage: a pound of silver was struck into 240 silver pennies, a system Britain kept until 1971. Alcuin of York ran the palace school, and monasteries copied books in a clear new script. This Carolingian minuscule is the ancestor of modern lower-case letters, and many works of Roman authors survive only because they were copied at this time.

steps: The empire divided

Charlemagne's son Louis the Pious inherited the empire, and Louis's three sons fought over it. The Treaty of Verdun in 843 split it in three: West, Middle and East Francia. The map's 900 snapshot shows the divided realm. West Francia became France, East Francia the German kingdom and the Holy Roman Empire, and the strip between them a borderland the two would contest for a thousand years.

p: Charlemagne died at Aachen in January 814, and his only surviving son, Louis, inherited the empire. Devout and determined to keep it whole, Louis decreed in 817 that his eldest son Lothar should have the imperial title and most of the lands, the two younger sons only border kingdoms. But his second wife bore him another son, the future Charles the Bald, and Louis's efforts to provide for the boy drove his older sons to rebel twice; in 833 they even deposed him for a time.

When Louis died in 840 Lothar claimed everything; his brothers Louis the German and Charles the Bald joined forces and crushed him in a bloody battle at Fontenoy in June 841. A year later the two swore oaths at Strasbourg in early Romance and Old High German, so each side's troops could understand; the Romance oath is often called the oldest text in French. In August 843 the brothers signed at Verdun: Charles took the west, Louis most of the lands east of the Rhine, and Lothar the imperial title and a long middle strip from the North Sea through Burgundy to Italy.

The middle kingdom broke up first. On Lothar's death it was split among his three sons; its northern part, named Lotharingia after Lothar II, later Lorraine, was divided between East and West in 870. Charles the Fat briefly reunited almost the whole empire in 884, but after he was deposed in 887 it fell apart for good. By 900 East Francia had a six-year-old king, Louis the Child, and the West Frankish crown had for a time passed to a non-Carolingian, Count Odo of Paris. Vikings, Magyars and Saracens raided from three sides, and local counts and dukes grew stronger.

plague.title: The Black Death
plague.lede: A plague that followed the trade routes across Europe in five years.
steps: From the Black Sea to Sicily

In 1346 an army of the Golden Horde besieging Caffa, the Genoese trading post in Crimea, was struck by plague. The next October, Genoese ships returning from the Black Sea docked at Messina in Sicily with sick men aboard. The plague had reached Europe.

p: The disease was plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and usually passed to humans by fleas from rats and other rodents. An ancient-DNA study published in 2022 found its ancestral strain in a cemetery of 1338–1339 in today's Kyrgyzstan, suggesting the outbreak began around the Tian Shan in Central Asia. Over the next few years it spread west along trade routes under Mongol control, and by 1346 it had reached the Golden Horde on the lower Volga and the northern shores of the Black Sea.

The army of the Golden Horde's khan Jani Beg was then besieging Caffa. According to the Italian notary Gabriele de' Mussis, the Mongols hurled plague corpses into the town with catapults, but he was not there and his is the only account. What is certain is that Genoese merchants fled by sea and, passing through Constantinople, carried the disease into the Mediterranean. In early October 1347 a fleet sailed into Messina; the Sicilian friar Michele da Piazza says it numbered 12 galleys.

The people of Messina soon drove the ships out, but it was too late. The disease spread through the city, then to Catania and across Sicily, while the expelled ships carried it to other ports. Victims' lymph nodes swelled in the groin or armpit, and many died within days; when the infection reached the lungs it could pass directly from person to person through coughing, and almost no one who caught that form survived. People at the time called it the great mortality; the name 'Black Death' caught on only centuries later.

steps: North along the trade routes

The plague followed Mediterranean shipping into Marseille, Genoa and Venice, then moved north along rivers and roads. In the spring of 1348 Florence lost about half its people within months, and that summer the plague reached Paris. The ten young people who flee to the countryside to tell stories in Boccaccio's Decameron are escaping this outbreak.

p: The plague landed at Marseille in November 1347 and by January 1348 had appeared in Pisa, Genoa and Venice. From Marseille it travelled up the Rhône, reaching Avignon, seat of the papacy, early in 1348. Pope Clement VI stayed in the city and bought land for a new cemetery; his physician Guy de Chauliac described the disease closely, distinguishing a form with swellings from one in which victims coughed blood. In July and September 1348 Clement issued bulls declaring the Jews blameless and forbidding attacks on them, with little effect.

Florence, one of Europe's largest cities with about 100,000 people, was struck in March or April, and the epidemic lasted until late summer. The rich fled to their country villas; those left behind died in droves, churchyards filled, and the dead were buried in layers in great trenches. The chronicler Giovanni Villani died of the plague himself: his chronicle breaks off with a blank left for the date when the epidemic would end. Boccaccio opened the Decameron with a long description of the horrors in the city.

Meanwhile the plague pushed north from the Mediterranean, along the Rhône and Saône and the roads to the northern fairs, into the heart of France. It reached Paris in the summer and was at its worst in the winter; a chronicle says the Hôtel-Dieu at times carried out hundreds of bodies a day. In October 1348 the medical faculty of the University of Paris, reporting at Philip VI's command, blamed a conjunction of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in 1345 for corrupting the air. Such explanations saved no one; people could only pray, flee or shut themselves away.

steps: Across the Channel

Around June 1348 the plague landed at a port in southern England and reached London before the year was out. The Hundred Years' War was not over, but the truce England and France had signed in 1347 was extended again and again because of the plague.

p: The Hundred Years' War had been going on for more than a decade. In August 1346 Edward III routed the French at Crécy, then besieged Calais for almost a year until it surrendered in August 1347. In September the two kingdoms agreed a truce through papal mediation. It was meant to run only until the following July, but the plague left neither side able to fight, and it was renewed again and again until war broke out afresh in 1355. In September 1348 Edward's daughter Joan, travelling to marry into the royal house of Castile, died of plague at Bordeaux.

The disease probably came on merchant ships from Gascony or Normandy; tradition puts the landing at Melcombe in Dorset, now part of Weymouth. It spread along the ports and roads, reaching Bristol in August and London in the autumn. New plague cemeteries were opened outside the city, as at East Smithfield, where archaeologists have since excavated hundreds of skeletons. In 1349 the plague swept the whole of England and moved on into Wales and Scotland.

Modern estimates put England's losses at between 30 and 50 per cent of the population. Clergy, who gave the last rites to the dying, died in especially large numbers; in 1349 two successive choices for Archbishop of Canterbury died of the plague. The Bishop of Bath and Wells even wrote that where no priest could be found, the dying might confess to a layman, or even to a woman. With labour scarce, wages rose, and in 1349 the king issued the Ordinance of Labourers, holding wages at pre-plague levels and storing up resentment between employers and workers.

steps: Into Scandinavia

In 1349 a ship from England brought the plague to Bergen in Norway, and from there it spread across Scandinavia. Norway's losses were especially heavy; some historians see them as one reason Norway stayed weak for a long time and became the junior partner in the Kalmar Union.

p: In 1349 the plague kept spreading through central Europe. Bands of flagellants appeared across Germany, marching from town to town and whipping themselves in public to turn aside God's anger; in October the pope banned the movement. Worse were the massacres of Jews, rumoured to have poisoned the wells: from Basel and Strasbourg to Mainz, Jewish communities were burned out, and in later years many Jews moved east to Poland.

Around the end of summer an English merchant ship put in at Bergen, and according to Icelandic annals it was this ship that brought the plague ashore. Bergen was Norway's largest town and the hub of its northern trade; from there the disease spread along the coast and fjords and soon covered the country, though some scholars think it had already reached the Oslo area in the autumn of 1348. From late 1349 into 1350 Denmark and Sweden were struck too, and King Magnus ordered fasting and penance throughout his realm. Remote Iceland escaped because shipping stopped, and met plague only in 1402.

Norway may have lost half its people or more. Farms were abandoned on a vast scale and many place names vanished. Rents collapsed, the nobility and Church were badly weakened, and native merchants declined, letting the German merchants of the Hanseatic League tighten their grip on Bergen's stockfish trade. Repeated outbreaks kept the population low for generations. From 1380 Norway shared a king with Denmark; after the Kalmar Union was formed in 1397 power lay on the Danish side, and the union of Norway and Denmark lasted until 1814.

steps: Five years on

Around 1352 the plague crossed the Baltic to Pskov and Novgorod, reaching Moscow the following year. Within a few years somewhere between a third and half of Europe's people had died. With labour suddenly scarce, surviving peasants and craftsmen could bargain for more, and in the following decades came the Jacquerie in France (1358) and the Peasants' Revolt in England (1381).

p: North-eastern Europe was the last region the plague reached. In 1352 it broke out in Pskov, killing many. The people of Pskov asked Archbishop Vasily of Novgorod to come and bless their city; he caught the disease on the way home and died, and the plague spread through Novgorod. In 1353 Grand Prince Simeon of Moscow, his two sons and one of his brothers all died of it, and the throne passed to another brother, Ivan II.

By then the first wave had long passed in western Europe. Modern scholars estimate that between 1347 and 1352 a third to a half of Europe's people died; with a pre-plague population of about 75 to 80 million, that means roughly 25 to 40 million deaths. Crowded places such as towns and monasteries often suffered worst, while a few areas escaped more lightly. Nor did the plague go away: it returned in 1361, 1369 and many times after, and Europe's population did not regain its pre-plague level until the late 15th century or later.

The shortage of labour changed the balance between lords and peasants. Across much of western Europe wages rose and rents fell; lords tried to force wages back down by law and raised taxes, breeding anger. In 1358 peasants in northern France attacked castles in the Jacquerie and were crushed by the nobility within weeks; in 1381 English peasants rose against the third poll tax and briefly took London. Both revolts failed, but serfdom slowly withered in the West. To keep plague out, Ragusa (today's Dubrovnik) ruled in 1377 that arrivals must spend 30 days in isolation, the beginning of quarantine.

thirty-years.title: The Thirty Years' War
thirty-years.lede: A religious quarrel that became a war remaking the European order.
steps: The window in Prague

In May 1618 Protestant nobles of Bohemia burst into Prague Castle and threw the Habsburg emperor's representatives out of a window. They were defying the rule of the Catholic Ferdinand over Bohemia. The revolt soon grew into a war across the Holy Roman Empire. The data draws the Empire as one block; in reality it was made up of hundreds of principalities, church lands and free cities.

p: Religious peace in the Holy Roman Empire rested on the Peace of Augsburg of 1555, which let each prince decide the faith of his lands but did not recognise Calvinism. By the early 1600s the princes had formed two rival camps, the Protestant Union and the Catholic League. Bohemia's Protestants held a charter granted by Emperor Rudolf II in 1609 guaranteeing their freedom of worship. But in 1617 the devout Catholic Ferdinand was accepted as King of Bohemia; one Protestant church was then closed and another demolished, and the nobles concluded that their rights were being taken away.

On 23 May 1618 Count Thurn led a band of Protestant nobles up to the castle, quarrelled with two regents, Slavata and Martinic, and pushed them out of a window along with a secretary. All three survived: Catholics credited the Virgin Mary, while Protestants said they had landed in a dung heap. The rebels set up a provisional government of 30 directors. In 1619 Emperor Matthias died and Ferdinand was elected emperor as Ferdinand II; almost simultaneously the Bohemian estates deposed him as their king and chose the Calvinist Frederick V, Elector Palatine, instead.

Frederick led the Protestant Union and was the son-in-law of James I of England; Ferdinand could count on his Spanish Habsburg cousins and the Bavarian-led Catholic League. A local act of defiance thus bound together the Empire's two religious camps and the interests of dynasties across Europe. The Empire's structure made the fire harder to put out: beneath the emperor stood seven electors and hundreds of principalities, church lands and free cities, each with its own troops and interests, and none able to settle matters alone.

steps: The Sack of Magdeburg

After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 the Bohemian revolt was crushed, and King Christian IV of Denmark, who intervened for the Protestant princes, was driven back in 1629. In 1631 imperial troops stormed the Protestant city of Magdeburg, and most of its people died in the massacre and fire. The atrocity pushed wavering Protestant princes such as Saxony and Brandenburg to side with Sweden.

p: On 8 November 1620 the imperial and Catholic League armies quickly routed the Bohemian army at White Mountain outside Prague. Frederick V fled and was mocked as the 'Winter King' for his single winter on the throne. In 1621, 27 rebel leaders were executed in Prague's Old Town Square and Protestantism in Bohemia was crushed; Frederick's own Palatinate was overrun by Spanish and Bavarian troops, and his electoral title passed to the Duke of Bavaria.

In 1625 King Christian IV of Denmark marched into northern Germany as protector of the Protestant cause. The emperor turned to the Bohemian nobleman Wallenstein, who raised an army tens of thousands strong largely at his own expense. Tilly, the Catholic League's commander, and Wallenstein won victory after victory, and Denmark left the war under the Peace of Lübeck in 1629. That same year Ferdinand II issued the Edict of Restitution, ordering Protestant princes to hand back church lands taken since 1552. Magdeburg, seat of an archbishopric long in Protestant hands, was directly threatened, and in 1630 it allied with Sweden.

In the spring of 1631 Tilly and Pappenheim laid siege to the city. Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden wanted to relieve it, but the Electors of Brandenburg and Saxony would not let his army through. On 20 May imperial troops broke in and fire swept through almost the whole city: of some 25,000 to 30,000 inhabitants, about 20,000 died. To 'magdeburgise' became a German byword for utter destruction. As the news spread, neutrality became impossible for the Protestant princes: Brandenburg, with Swedish guns at its gates, made a full alliance in June, and Saxony joined Sweden in September after Tilly invaded it.

steps: The Lion of the North

King Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania in 1630, crushed the imperial army at Breitenfeld the following year and drove deep into southern Germany. At Lützen in 1632 Sweden won the battle, but the king was killed. Sweden's war had an unexpected paymaster: Catholic France.

p: Gustavus Adolphus went to war in Germany to protect Protestantism, but even more to secure Sweden's position on the Baltic: Wallenstein's armies had already reached the Baltic coast. In 1629 French mediation brought a truce between Sweden and Poland that freed the king's hands. In July 1630 he landed with about 13,000 men. Under the Treaty of Bärwalde, signed the following January, France would pay 400,000 thalers a year, and Sweden would keep 36,000 men in Germany and respect Catholic worship there.

On 17 September 1631 the Swedes and Saxons met Tilly at Breitenfeld, north of Leipzig. The Saxons broke at the first shock, but the Swedes held firm with their flexible small brigades and light field guns, then counter-attacked; the imperial army lost more than 10,000 killed, wounded or captured. It was the Protestants' first great victory. Gustavus marched west to winter at Mainz on the Rhine; in spring 1632 he invaded Bavaria, Tilly was mortally wounded in battle on the Lech, and in May the Swedes entered Munich. The emperor had to recall Wallenstein, dismissed in 1630.

Wallenstein drove into Saxony and forced Gustavus north to fight. On 16 November 1632 the armies met at Lützen, south-west of Leipzig. In thick fog the king, leading a cavalry charge, became separated from his men and was shot from his horse; he was 37. Bernhard of Saxe-Weimar took command and held the field, and Wallenstein withdrew to Bohemia. Sweden had won the battle but lost its leader. His daughter Christina was not yet six, and the chancellor Axel Oxenstierna took charge of the state and of a war that depended more and more on French money.

steps: France joins in

In 1635 France declared war on Spain and then on the emperor. Catholic France under Cardinal Richelieu fought alongside Protestant Sweden against the equally Catholic Habsburgs. By now the war was no longer mainly about religion; it was a contest for supremacy in Europe between the Bourbon and Habsburg dynasties.

p: After Gustavus's death the tide turned. In February 1634 Wallenstein, suspected of secret dealings with the enemy, was stripped of his command and murdered by his own officers at Eger. That September the emperor's son Ferdinand, reinforced by a Spanish army, crushed the Swedes at Nördlingen; the Swedish side lost more than 10,000 killed, wounded or captured, and its hold on southern Germany collapsed. On 30 May 1635 the emperor and Saxony signed the Peace of Prague, suspending the Edict of Restitution, and most Protestant princes soon accepted it. The war inside Germany looked close to ending.

Richelieu could not allow that. Spain, the Spanish Netherlands and Spanish Franche-Comté lay to France's south, north and east: Habsburg lands and military roads all but encircled the kingdom, and a revived emperor allied to Spain would be a mortal danger. In April 1635 France renewed its alliance with Sweden, and on 19 May a French herald declared war on Spain in Brussels in the old medieval manner. Soon France also hired Bernhard's army and fought the imperial forces directly along the Rhine.

The French war began badly. In 1636 a Spanish army marched south from the Netherlands and took Corbie on the Somme, and Paris was briefly gripped by panic. But France steadied. In 1638 Bernhard took the Rhine fortress of Breisach, cutting Spain's military road to the Netherlands, and in 1643 the Duke of Enghien routed the Spanish infantry at Rocroi. The war became a long grind of foreign armies on German soil. Troops lived off the land and made the war feed itself; famine and plague followed, and far more civilians died of disease and hunger than soldiers in battle.

steps: The Peace of Westphalia

In 1648 the warring parties signed peace treaties at Münster and Osnabrück. The independence of the Dutch Republic and of Switzerland was recognised; the princes of the Empire gained the right to make alliances and run their own foreign policy, further hollowing out the emperor's authority; and Calvinism gained the same legal standing as Catholicism and Lutheranism. The population of the German lands is estimated to have fallen by about a fifth overall, and by more than half in some regions.

p: Delegates had begun arriving in Westphalia in 1643, and the talks ran for about five years. Because Catholics and Protestants would not meet in the same town, the congress sat in two cities some 50 km apart: in Münster the emperor negotiated with France, in Osnabrück with Sweden and the Protestant estates. Away from the table the fighting went on. In the summer of 1648 Swedish troops stormed the Lesser Town of Prague and plundered the castle's treasures, so the war ended where it had begun.

In January 1648 Spain and the Dutch signed their own treaty at Münster: Spain formally recognised the Dutch Republic, ending eighty years of war. On 24 October the Empire's treaties with France and Sweden were signed. Sweden received Western Pomerania, Wismar, and Bremen and Verden, plus 5 million thalers to pay off its army; France gained the three bishoprics of Metz, Toul and Verdun and the Habsburgs' rights in Alsace. Frederick V's son regained the Rhenish Palatinate and a new, eighth electorate. The princes' right of alliance came with a condition: no alliance could be aimed at the emperor or the Empire.

The peace did not end all war: France and Spain fought on until 1659. But it set new rules. States large and small sat at one conference table and fixed borders and rights by treaty, while the Empire came to resemble a loose association of princes; later generations often saw this as the starting point of the modern system of sovereign states. The cost was appalling. The population of the German lands fell by about a fifth overall; Mecklenburg, Pomerania and Württemberg suffered worst, and recovery took generations.

steps: The new map

This step switches to the 1650 snapshot; the hatching marks land that changed hands since the previous one. Sweden was the biggest winner. Western Pomerania, granted by the peace, is only a small piece; more came from Denmark-Norway (1645), Poland-Lithuania (1629) and Russia (1617) during the war. Switzerland's separation from the Empire is on the map too. France's gains of Metz, Toul, Verdun and rights in Alsace are not drawn in this data.

p: Sweden, a northern kingdom of only a million or so people, emerged from the Thirty Years' War as a great power. Its expansion had begun before it entered the war. The Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617 gave it Ingria and part of Karelia from Russia, shutting Russia out of the Baltic; the Truce of Altmark in 1629 left Sweden holding most of Livonia, including Riga.

In 1643 Sweden suddenly turned its army north from Germany against Denmark, in a war that lasted two years. The Peace of Brömsebro in 1645 gave Sweden the islands of Gotland and Ösel and the Norwegian provinces of Jämtland and Härjedalen, and handed it Halland for 30 years. Three years later the Peace of Westphalia added Western Pomerania, Wismar, and Bremen and Verden. The mouths of three great rivers, the Oder, the Elbe and the Weser, were now under Swedish control, and the Baltic was close to becoming a Swedish lake. As ruler of these lands, the Swedish king also gained seats in the Imperial Diet.

The other winners changed the map too. The independence of Switzerland and the Dutch Republic was formally recognised. Brandenburg gained Eastern Pomerania, Halberstadt and Minden, as well as the right to inherit Magdeburg, laying the foundations for the later rise of Prussia. France pushed its border towards the Rhine and gradually replaced Spain as the leading power on the Continent. The Habsburg emperors turned their attention back to Austria, Bohemia and Hungary. For the next century and a half the Empire never recovered its old authority.

napoleon.title: The Age of Napoleon
napoleon.lede: From the Bastille to Waterloo: twenty-six years that redrew Europe.
steps: Storming of the Bastille

On 14 July 1789 the people of Paris stormed the Bastille, a symbol of royal power. Bankruptcy, soaring bread prices and Enlightenment ideas quickly turned the Estates-General into a revolution against the old order. In 1792 France went to war with Austria and Prussia and declared a republic the same year.

p: The revolution began with money. Two expensive wars, the Seven Years' War and the American War of Independence, had left France deep in debt, and by the late 1780s interest payments swallowed nearly half the crown's revenue. When Louis XVI tried to tax the nobility and clergy they refused, and in May 1789 he had to summon the Estates-General, which had not met for 175 years. The deputies of the Third Estate soon declared themselves the National Assembly and swore, in a tennis court, not to disband until France had a constitution.

In mid-July the king massed troops around Paris and dismissed his popular finance minister, Jacques Necker, and Parisians expected a crackdown. On the 14th crowds seized muskets from the Invalides and went to the Bastille for gunpowder. The garrison opened fire; after several hours of fighting the fortress surrendered and its governor was killed. It held only seven prisoners, but the grim fortress stood for the king's power to imprison without trial, and its fall became the symbol of the old regime's collapse.

What followed came astonishingly fast. On the night of 4 August the Assembly abolished feudal privileges, and on 26 August it adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Europe's monarchs were amused at first, then alarmed. France declared war on Austria in April 1792 and Prussia joined in; in September the republic was proclaimed, and in January 1793 Louis XVI went to the guillotine. To face enemies on every side, the republic introduced mass conscription in 1793 and raised the largest army in Europe, the army Napoleon would later wield.

steps: Egypt

The young artillery officer Napoleon Bonaparte made his name in the Italian campaign of 1796. In 1798 he led an expedition to Egypt to cut Britain's route to India, but his fleet was destroyed by Nelson at Aboukir Bay. The next year he left his army behind, returned to France, seized power in the coup of 18 Brumaire and became First Consul.

p: Napoleon was born on Corsica in 1769, a year after France acquired the island. Trained as an artillery officer, he drove the British out of Toulon with his guns in 1793 and became a brigadier general at 24. In 1796 he took over the ragged Army of Italy, beat Sardinia and Austria within a year and forced Austria into the Treaty of Campo Formio, which handed Belgium to France. He came back to Paris the most famous general in the country, a man the Directory both relied on and feared.

Britain was the one enemy still standing, and a crossing of the Channel looked too risky, so Napoleon proposed Egypt instead: seize the gateway to India and build French power in the East. The fleet left Toulon in May 1798, took Malta on the way and landed at Alexandria in July, and at the Battle of the Pyramids the army broke the Mamluk cavalry. But on the night of 1 August Nelson fell on the French fleet at anchor in Aboukir Bay. Of 13 ships of the line only 2 escaped, and more than 30,000 French soldiers were stranded in Egypt.

The expedition also carried more than 160 scholars, who surveyed the Nile valley and studied its monuments; in 1799 soldiers at Rosetta dug up a stone inscribed in three scripts that would become the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs. Militarily the campaign sank deeper: a march into Syria stalled before Acre, and plague broke out in the army. In August 1799 Napoleon handed over command and slipped home by sea. The coup came on 9 November, 18 Brumaire in the revolutionary calendar; five years later, in December 1804, he was crowned emperor in Notre-Dame.
facts: 2 of 13 French ships of the line escaped

steps: Sea and land

Napoleon crowned himself emperor in 1804. In October 1805 the British fleet crushed the Franco-Spanish fleet at Trafalgar and took firm command of the sea; just over a month later Napoleon routed the Russians and Austrians at Austerlitz. The pattern of the next decade was set: Britain ruled the seas, France ruled the Continent.

p: Britain and France made peace at Amiens in 1802, but it lasted little more than a year. Napoleon gathered nearly 200,000 men at Boulogne to invade England, provided his fleet could hold the Channel for even a few days. In 1805 Britain drew Austria, Russia and Sweden into the Third Coalition. With the crossing out of reach, Napoleon turned east: his army marched from the Channel to the Danube and in October surrounded the Austrians at Ulm, where General Mack surrendered with more than 20,000 men.

On 21 October, the day after Ulm fell, Nelson took 27 ships of the line against 33 French and Spanish ships off Cape Trafalgar in Spain. He drove two columns straight into the middle of the enemy line; after five hours of fighting 22 allied ships had been captured or destroyed, and Britain had lost none. Nelson himself was shot dead. For the next hundred years no power could challenge Britain at sea.

On land it was another story. On 2 December, the first anniversary of his coronation, about 73,000 French faced about 85,000 Russians and Austrians at Austerlitz in Moravia, with Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II both on the field: the Battle of the Three Emperors. Napoleon gave up the Pratzen Heights and showed a weak right wing; when the allies swung south to envelop it, he stormed the heights in the centre and cut their army in two. The allies lost about 27,000 men, the French fewer than 9,000. Three weeks later Austria signed the Peace of Pressburg, gave up Venetia and the Tyrol, and left the war.
facts: 27 British vs 33 Franco-Spanish ships of the line

steps: End of an empire

In 1806 Napoleon gathered the states of southwestern Germany into the Confederation of the Rhine under his protection, and Francis II gave up the title of Holy Roman Emperor, ending an empire of more than 800 years. That autumn Prussia was beaten at both Jena and Auerstedt. This data has no snapshot between 1800 and 1815, so these changes do not yet appear on the map.

p: After Austerlitz the old order in Germany could not hold. In July 1806 sixteen states, among them Bavaria, Württemberg and Baden, left the Holy Roman Empire to form the Confederation of the Rhine, with Napoleon as its 'protector' and the states supplying his troops. On 6 August Francis II laid down the title of Holy Roman Emperor, keeping only the title of Emperor of Austria he had taken two years before. Counted from Otto I's coronation in 962, the empire had lasted 844 years.

Prussia had stayed neutral in 1805; with French power now at its door, it went to war in the autumn of 1806. On a single day, 14 October, Napoleon beat part of the Prussian army at Jena while Marshal Davout, outnumbered, routed its main body at Auerstedt some twenty kilometres away. The army of Frederick the Great collapsed in a day, and two weeks later Napoleon rode into Berlin. There he issued the Berlin Decree banning trade between the Continent and Britain: the Continental System.

In 1807 the French beat the Russians at Friedland, and Napoleon and Alexander I met on a raft in the middle of the Neman to make the Treaties of Tilsit. Prussia lost about half its territory and population: its western lands went to the new Kingdom of Westphalia, and its share of partitioned Poland became the Duchy of Warsaw. This was the height of Napoleon's power; from Spain to Poland the great powers of the Continent were either beaten or allied to him.
facts: lost about half its land and people

steps: The invasion of Russia

In June 1812 Napoleon crossed the Neman with about 600,000 men. The Russians fell back, fought a bloody battle at Borodino in September and then abandoned Moscow. After the French entered, Moscow burned and the tsar refused to negotiate. The winter retreat all but destroyed the army; only a few tens of thousands of fighting men were left.

p: The Continental System hurt Britain, but it hurt Europe too. Russia depended on British markets for its grain and timber, and at the end of 1810 Alexander I opened his ports to neutral ships and raised duties on French goods, in effect leaving the blockade. Meanwhile Napoleon was bogged down in an endless guerrilla war in Spain that tied up 200,000 to 300,000 of his troops. He decided to force the tsar back into the alliance with one decisive battle.

On 24 June 1812 the Grande Armée crossed the Neman about 600,000 strong, about half of them Germans, Poles, Italians and other allied or subject troops. The Russians refused battle and fell back, stripping the country as they went. Only on 7 September did Kutuzov make a stand at Borodino, a little over 100 km west of Moscow. That day cost the two armies about 70,000 casualties, one of the bloodiest days of the Napoleonic Wars. The Russians then withdrew, and on 14 September the French entered an almost deserted Moscow.

That night fires broke out and burned for days until three-quarters of the city was ash. Napoleon waited five weeks in the Kremlin; the tsar never answered. On 19 October the French began to retreat, with winter closing in, supplies gone and Cossacks harrying the columns, and they lost heavily again forcing the Berezina at the end of November. Of the more than 400,000 men in Napoleon's main army, only a few tens of thousands struggled out. As the news spread, Prussia and then Austria changed sides. The fall of the empire began here.
facts: about 600,000 men, half of them from allied or subject states

steps: The order of Vienna

In 1814 the allies entered Paris and Napoleon was exiled to Elba; he returned the next year and was finally defeated at Waterloo after a hundred days. Look at the hatching on the 1815 snapshot: Russia had taken Finland from Sweden in 1809 and won most of Poland at the Congress of Vienna, Norway passed from Denmark to Sweden, and Prussia gained the northern half of Saxony. Europe would not see another war engulfing the whole continent for nearly a century.

p: In October 1813 the Russians, Prussians, Austrians and Swedes met Napoleon at Leipzig. More than 500,000 men fought in this 'Battle of the Nations', the largest battle in Europe before the First World War. Beaten, the French fell back across the Rhine. On 31 March 1814 the allies marched into Paris; Napoleon abdicated and was sent to Elba in the Mediterranean, and the Bourbon Louis XVIII took the throne.

The victors' monarchs and ministers then gathered in Vienna to redraw Europe. The leading parts went to Austria's Metternich, Britain's Castlereagh and Tsar Alexander I, and to Talleyrand, who represented defeated France and played the others off against each other. Midway through, in March 1815, Napoleon slipped back from Elba and reached Paris without a shot fired: the Hundred Days. On 18 June he met Wellington's British and allied army at Waterloo in Belgium; in the evening Blücher's Prussians came up on his flank and the French army broke. Napoleon abdicated again and was exiled to St Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.

The Congress signed its Final Act nine days before Waterloo. Its principles were legitimate dynasties and a balance among the great powers. The Holy Roman Empire was not revived; in its place came a loose German Confederation of 39 states. The Netherlands and Belgium were joined in one kingdom to guard France's northern border; Prussia gained the Rhineland and half of Saxony; Austria took back Lombardy and Venetia; Russia received most of Poland as a kingdom with the tsar as its king. The five great powers then met regularly. This 'Concert of Europe' smothered national and liberal movements, but for decades afterwards the great powers settled most of their quarrels at the conference table.

ww1.title: The First World War
ww1.lede: One shot, and four empires fell.
steps: Shots in Sarajevo

On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to Austria-Hungary, was assassinated in Sarajevo by the Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip. Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia, Russia mobilised in Serbia's support, Germany declared war on Russia and France and attacked France through Belgium, and Britain joined in. Within about five weeks the alliance system had dragged all of Europe into war.

p: The Balkans were the most unstable corner of Europe. Austria-Hungary had occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1878 and annexed it outright in 1908, enraging Serbia, since many Serbs lived there. The two Balkan Wars almost doubled Serbia's territory, and Vienna came to see it as a mortal threat. The great powers stood in two blocs: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy formed the Triple Alliance, while France, Russia and Britain made up the Triple Entente.

On 28 June, after attending army manoeuvres, Franz Ferdinand visited Sarajevo with his wife Sophie. A bomb thrown at their motorcade that morning missed. Later the car took a wrong turn and stopped to reverse near the Latin Bridge, and the 19-year-old Princip shot them both dead at close range. The assassins belonged to Young Bosnia and had been armed by the Black Hand, a secret society run by Serbian army officers. In early July Germany promised Austria-Hungary unconditional support, the so-called blank cheque. On 23 July Vienna sent Serbia an ultimatum with a 48-hour deadline; Serbia accepted most of its terms, but not all. On 28 July, exactly a month after the shooting, Austria-Hungary declared war.

The chain reaction took just a week. Russia ordered general mobilisation on 30 July; Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, and marched into Belgium as planned. Britain, citing the treaty of 1839 that guaranteed Belgian neutrality, declared war on Germany on 4 August. Italy stayed out, arguing that its alliance was purely defensive. Many expected a war of a few months; few foresaw that it would last more than four years and kill about ten million soldiers.

steps: The Western Front

Following the Schlieffen Plan, German armies swept through Belgium hoping to defeat France within six weeks. At the Marne in September the French and British stopped them east of Paris. The trenches then ran from the North Sea to the Swiss border, and for more than three years the front barely moved.

p: Germany's great fear was a war on two fronts. Schlieffen, chief of the general staff, drew up a plan around 1905 that relied on Russia's slow mobilisation: the army would mass on its right wing, swing through Belgium, envelop Paris and knock France out in about six weeks, then turn east. German troops entered Belgium on 4 August, smashed the Liège forts with giant siege guns and burned the university library at Leuven; reports of murdered civilians shocked neutral countries. The French, following Plan XVII, attacked into Alsace and Lorraine; in the Battle of the Frontiers machine guns and artillery cut them down, and on 22 August alone about 27,000 French soldiers died.

The German right wing pressed on towards Paris. But the Germans were tiring, and Russia's early invasion of East Prussia led Moltke the Younger to send two corps east. Kluck's First Army, chasing the Allies, wheeled to pass east of Paris and exposed its flank. In early September the French commander, Joffre, ordered a general counter-offensive, and Paris taxis rushed reinforcements to the front overnight. The Germans fell back to the Aisne and dug in. The Schlieffen Plan had failed, and Moltke was dismissed.

Each side then tried to outflank the other to the north, in the Race to the Sea. At Ypres in October and November Britain's old regular army was all but wiped out, and the Belgians opened the sluices on the Yser to halt the Germans with floodwater. By the end of 1914 a line of trenches about 700 km long ran from the North Sea to the Swiss border. Barbed wire, machine guns and artillery made defence far easier than attack.
facts: defeat France in about six weeks

steps: Two camps

Highlighted are the Central Powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and, from 1915, Bulgaria. Facing them were the Allies, France, Britain and Russia, later joined by Italy and Romania, with the United States entering the war in 1917. In 1916 Verdun cost hundreds of thousands of casualties and the Somme more than a million, and neither broke the deadlock.

p: The two camps formed during the war itself. In the autumn of 1914 the Ottoman Empire sided with Germany and closed the Straits, cutting Russia's shortest sea link with its allies. Italy, formally in the Triple Alliance, changed sides in May 1915 once the Allies promised it Austro-Hungarian land. That October Bulgaria joined the Central Powers and helped overrun Serbia. The Central Powers were blockaded by the Royal Navy throughout.

In 1915 the Allies attacked the Dardanelles. On 18 March British and French battleships tried to force the narrows, and three struck mines and sank. On 25 April British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula, but were pinned to the beaches and hillsides by the Ottomans; a young officer, Mustafa Kemal, made his name there. After more than eight months of stalemate the Allies withdrew completely in January 1916. Winston Churchill, its champion, had already lost his post as First Lord of the Admiralty in May 1915.

In 1916 two great battles in the West took attrition to the extreme. On 21 February the German chief of staff, Falkenhayn, attacked at Verdun, aiming, by his own later account, to make the French pour in men until they bled to death. Under Pétain the French held, supplied along a single road known as the Sacred Way. The battle lasted nearly ten months, cost over 700,000 casualties on both sides and left the line almost where it began. On 1 July the Allies attacked on the Somme; the British suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day, nearly 20,000 of them killed. By November casualties on both sides exceeded a million, and the Allies had advanced about 10 km at most.

steps: Russia drops out

The war broke tsarist Russia. The February Revolution of 1917 overthrew the tsar, and in the October Revolution the Bolsheviks seized power. In March 1918 Soviet Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with the Central Powers, giving up control of Finland, the Baltic lands, Poland and Ukraine.

p: The war laid bare Russia's weaknesses. At Tannenberg in 1914 a whole Russian army was all but destroyed, and the Great Retreat of 1915 cost the whole of Poland. Tsar Nicholas II went to the front as commander-in-chief, leaving the capital to the empress and her favourite, Rasputin, and government sank into chaos. By early 1917 Russia's killed, wounded and captured ran into the millions, the cities were short of bread, prices soared and soldiers deserted in droves.

On 8 March 1917 (23 February old style) women in Petrograd marched for bread. Strikes and protests spread, and troops sent to crush them joined the crowds. On 15 March Nicholas II abdicated, ending more than 300 years of Romanov rule. The Provisional Government fought on, but its July offensive ended in disaster. Germany arranged for Lenin, in exile in Switzerland, to return home by train, and his slogan of 'peace, land and bread' won over war-weary soldiers and workers. On 7 November (25 October old style) Red Guards and soldiers led by Trotsky seized key points in Petrograd, stormed the Winter Palace and toppled the government.

The next day the new regime issued its Decree on Peace, and in December it agreed an armistice with the Central Powers. Germany's terms were harsh; talks broke down and German armies surged forward. Lenin insisted on accepting, and on 3 March 1918 the treaty was signed at Brest-Litovsk. Soviet Russia lost between a quarter and a third of its population, most of its coal mines and much of its industry, and moved its capital from Petrograd to safer Moscow. With the East closed, Germany could shift large forces west for a final throw.

steps: Armistice

In the spring of 1918 Germany launched a last great offensive in the West; when it failed, it could no longer go on. Bulgaria, the Ottomans and Austria-Hungary sued for peace one after another, revolution broke out in Germany and the Kaiser abdicated. On 11 November the armistice was signed in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne. About ten million soldiers had died.

p: In February 1917 Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare; together with the Zimmermann Telegram, this brought the United States into the war in April. Ludendorff, Germany's effective commander, decided to strike in the West before the Americans arrived in strength, with divisions freed from the East. Operation Michael opened on 21 March 1918. With storm-troop infiltration tactics the Germans tore open the British line and within a fortnight advanced up to about 60 km, the biggest breakthrough in the West since 1914.

But each German blow was weaker than the last; losses went unreplaced and supplies ran short. The Allies united their command under Foch, and Americans were reaching France at hundreds of thousands a month. After the Second Marne in July the Allies held the initiative. On 8 August the British attacked at Amiens with masses of tanks, a day Ludendorff later called the black day of the German army. In the Hundred Days Offensive that followed the Allies broke the Hindenburg Line, and on 29 September Ludendorff told the government to seek an armistice at once.

Germany's allies gave way first: Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September, the Ottomans on 30 October, and Austria-Hungary on 3 November. In early November sailors mutinied at Kiel and revolution spread; on 9 November Berlin announced the Kaiser's abdication and proclaimed a republic, and Wilhelm II fled to the Netherlands. The armistice was signed early on 11 November, and at 11 a.m. the guns fell silent. Germany had to leave the occupied lands and Alsace-Lorraine, hand over masses of weapons, give up its fleet for internment and renounce the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Of the soldiers killed, about 2 million were German and 1.4 million French.

steps: The ruins of empire

The hatching on the 1920 snapshot covers almost all of Central and Eastern Europe. The monarchies of the German, Austro-Hungarian and Russian empires had fallen, the Ottoman Empire was being carved up by the victors, and Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia (then the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes) and the three Baltic states appeared on the map. Many new borders left minorities inside other states, sowing the seeds of the next war twenty years later.

p: The Paris Peace Conference opened in January 1919. President Wilson of the United States came with his Fourteen Points, calling for borders drawn along national lines; the French premier, Clemenceau, was set on weakening Germany; the British prime minister, Lloyd George, had aims of his own. On 28 June 1919, five years to the day after Sarajevo, German delegates signed the treaty in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles.

Germany lost about 13 per cent of its territory and 10 per cent of its population. Alsace-Lorraine returned to France; Posen and most of West Prussia went to Poland, forming a corridor to the Baltic, and Danzig became a free city. The Saar was placed under the League of Nations for 15 years, and the Rhineland was demilitarised and occupied by the Allies. The army was capped at 100,000 men, with no air force or submarines, and all colonies were lost. The treaty included a war-guilt clause, and reparations were later set at 132 billion gold marks. Other defeated states signed separate treaties; the Treaty of Trianon of 4 June 1920 stripped Hungary of about two-thirds of its territory, leaving about 3 million Hungarians outside its borders.

In 1920 Soviet Russia signed treaties recognising the three Baltic states, while reborn Poland fought Soviet Russia and threw back the Red Army before Warsaw in August. The Ottoman Empire was carved up by the Treaty of Sèvres in 1920, and its sultanate was abolished two years later. The new borders rarely matched where peoples lived: Czechoslovakia held about 3 million Germans, and Romania gained Transylvania with its large Hungarian population. Such grievances later became weapons for Nazi Germany and other revisionist powers.

iron-curtain.title: The Iron Curtain
iron-curtain.lede: Four decades of division, then half a continent redrawn in a few years.
steps: Postwar lines

Germany surrendered in May 1945. The hatching shows what changed: Germany was split into American, British, French and Soviet occupation zones; the Soviet border moved west, taking in the three Baltic states, eastern Poland and Romanian Bessarabia; Poland shifted west as a whole, gaining Germany's eastern lands. With Soviet backing, Communist parties took power across Eastern Europe over the next few years.

p: From 4 to 11 February 1945 President Roosevelt, Prime Minister Churchill and the Soviet leader Stalin met at Yalta in the Crimea. They agreed to divide Germany into occupation zones; Poland's eastern border would broadly follow the Curzon Line, and Poland would be compensated with German land in the west; the liberated countries of Europe would form governments through free elections.

On 16 April Soviet armies under Zhukov and Konev opened the Battle of Berlin. Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April, and the city's garrison surrendered on 2 May. Germany signed an unconditional surrender at Reims on 7 May and again in Berlin on 8 May, the day it took effect. About 80,000 Soviet soldiers were killed in the battle for Berlin. The Potsdam Conference in July and August confirmed four-power rule over Germany through a Control Council, with Berlin likewise divided; German land east of the Oder–Neisse line went under Polish administration, and Königsberg went to the Soviet Union, later renamed Kaliningrad.

The new borders set off vast movements of people. Some 12 to 14 million Germans fled or were expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia and elsewhere, and over a million Poles moved west from lands annexed by the Soviet Union. With Soviet backing, Communist parties across Eastern Europe took power step by step: between 1946 and 1948 the opposition was pushed aside in Poland, Romania, Hungary and Bulgaria, and in February 1948 the Communists took full control of Czechoslovakia. In March 1946, in a speech at Fulton in the United States, Churchill declared that from Stettin on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic an iron curtain had descended across the Continent.

steps: One city, two worlds

In 1949 the western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany and the Soviet zone the German Democratic Republic. Berlin, inside East Germany, was split as well. By 1961 two to three million East Germans had fled to the West, most of them through Berlin. That August, East Germany sealed the border overnight and then built the Berlin Wall.

p: Berlin was the Cold War's first flashpoint. In June 1948 the western zones introduced a currency reform with a new Deutsche Mark and extended it to West Berlin. The Soviet Union then cut the rail, road and water routes into the western sectors. The Americans and British organised an airlift that ran from June 1948 to September 1949: some 278,000 flights carried about 2.3 million tonnes of food, coal and other supplies, keeping more than two million West Berliners alive. The Soviets lifted the blockade in May 1949.

The gap between the two Germanys kept widening. West Germany's economy recovered rapidly, while East Germany imposed central planning and collective farming, and a workers' uprising on 17 June 1953 was crushed by Soviet tanks. The border between the two states was closed in 1952, but people could still move freely between the sectors of Berlin; a ride on the underground led to the West. Between 1949 and 1961 about 2.7 million people left East Germany, many of them young people, doctors, engineers and skilled workers; in July 1961 alone about 30,000 fled.

That June the East German leader, Walter Ulbricht, had told a press conference: 'No one has the intention of building a wall.' In the early hours of 13 August soldiers and police strung barbed wire along the sector boundary and closed the streets, and within days work began on a concrete wall, which East Germany called the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart. In October American and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie for about 16 hours. The barrier around West Berlin eventually ran to about 155 km, and by 1989 at least 140 people had died at the Wall.

steps: Reform under the tanks

The Soviet Union would not let Eastern Europe slip out of its grip. The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 was put down by Soviet troops. In 1968 the Czechoslovak leader Alexander Dubček pursued socialism with a human face, and that August Warsaw Pact armies rolled into Prague and ended the reforms.

p: Stalin died in 1953. In February 1956 Khrushchev's secret speech to the Twentieth Party Congress denounced Stalin's personality cult, and Eastern Europe began to stir. In June workers in Poznań, Poland, took to the streets; in October Władysław Gomułka returned as Poland's leader, and Moscow eventually accepted this. On 23 October students and citizens in Budapest marched, demanding the withdrawal of Soviet troops and free elections, and the clashes quickly grew into a national uprising.

The reformer Imre Nagy became prime minister, announced a multi-party system and on 1 November declared Hungary's withdrawal from the Warsaw Pact and its neutrality. On 4 November Soviet forces poured into Budapest and crushed resistance within days. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed and about 200,000 fled abroad. Nagy was arrested, tried in secret and executed in 1958. Western governments sympathised but did not intervene; Britain and France were then embroiled in the Suez Crisis.

In January 1968 Alexander Dubček became first secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party. Censorship was eased and open debate allowed, and public life flourished in what became known as the Prague Spring. Repeated pressure from the Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev failed. Late on 20 August several hundred thousand troops from the Soviet Union, Poland, Hungary, Bulgaria and other states crossed the border and by the next day held Prague. Dubček was taken to Moscow to sign a protocol; in April 1969 he was replaced by Gustáv Husák, and the reforms were rolled back. In the West the Soviet stance became known as the Brezhnev Doctrine: the interests of the socialist camp as a whole came before national sovereignty. Romania refused to take part, and Albania soon left the Warsaw Pact.

steps: Strike in Gdańsk

In August 1980 workers at the Gdańsk shipyard went on strike, and the electrician Lech Wałęsa led the founding of Solidarity, an independent trade union that soon had about ten million members. The government declared martial law in 1981 and Solidarity went underground, but it did not disappear.

p: Polish workers had a tradition of protest: in Poznań in 1956, in the Baltic ports in 1970 and in Radom in 1976 there were strikes and riots, and the crackdown of 1970 left dozens dead. In the 1970s the Polish leader Edward Gierek borrowed heavily from the West; by 1980 foreign debt had passed 20 billion dollars and shortages were worsening. In 1978 Karol Wojtyła, Archbishop of Kraków, was elected pope as John Paul II, and when he visited Poland the next year millions attended his open-air masses.

In July 1980 meat prices rose again and strikes broke out across the country. On 14 August workers at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk downed tools over the dismissal of the crane operator Anna Walentynowicz. Lech Wałęsa, himself sacked earlier for union activity, climbed over the shipyard wall and became the strike leader. The strike spread along the coast, and the workers drew up 21 demands, the first of which was for free trade unions independent of the party. On 31 August the government signed the Gdańsk Agreement, accepting it. In September Solidarity was formally founded.

Solidarity's members made up about a third of the country's workforce, and it was the first legal independent trade union in a Communist state. Soviet forces held manoeuvres near Poland's borders, and tension mounted. On 13 December 1981 Poland's leader, General Wojciech Jaruzelski, declared martial law; thousands of Solidarity activists, Wałęsa among them, were interned, and in 1982 the union was formally banned. But it carried on underground, and in 1983 Wałęsa was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. By 1989 the movement would be back at centre stage.

steps: In 1989 the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev gave up using force to control Eastern Europe. Solidarity swept the June elections in Poland, Hungary took down the fence on its Austrian border, and East Germans fled through it in their thousands. On the night of 9 November the Berlin Wall opened and people climbed onto it. Before the year was out, the regimes in Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Romania had fallen too.

p: Mikhail Gorbachev, in power since 1985, faced a stagnant economy, a crushing military budget and the drain of the war in Afghanistan, and launched perestroika and glasnost. In December 1988 he told the United Nations that the Soviet Union would cut its forces unilaterally by 500,000 men, and that every people had the right to choose its own path. Eastern Europe's ruling parties had lost their last guarantee.

Poland led the way. After Round Table talks the government agreed to partly free elections. In the June elections Solidarity won all 161 contested seats in the lower house and 99 of the 100 seats in the new Senate; in August Solidarity's Tadeusz Mazowiecki became prime minister, the first non-Communist head of government in the Eastern bloc. Hungary began dismantling its border fence in May and in September opened the border to East Germans; tens of thousands crossed via Austria to West Germany. Protest swelled in East Germany: on 9 October some 70,000 people marched in Leipzig, and on 18 October Erich Honecker was ousted.

On the evening of 9 November the East German official Günter Schabowski announced relaxed travel rules at a press conference; asked when they took effect, he wrongly answered 'immediately'. Tens of thousands of East Berliners converged on the checkpoints, and late that night the guards gave way. Change came fast: Bulgaria's leader Todor Zhivkov fell on 10 November; Czechoslovakia's Velvet Revolution began on 17 November, and on 29 December Václav Havel was elected president; in Romania fighting erupted in December, killing about 1,100 people, and Nicolae Ceaușescu and his wife fled, were captured and were executed on 25 December. Romania's was the year's only bloody change of regime.

steps: New borders

Germany reunited in 1990; at the end of 1991 the Soviet Union dissolved and its fifteen republics became independent; Yugoslavia broke apart in war; and in 1993 Czechoslovakia split peacefully. The hatching on the 1994 snapshot marks these changes: from the Baltic to the Black Sea and the Caucasus, the political map of the eastern half of Europe was redrawn within a few years.

p: German unity came faster than expected. East Germany held its first free elections in March 1990, and in July the two states formed a monetary union. In September they signed the Two Plus Four Treaty with the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France: a united Germany would accept the Oder–Neisse border and cap its forces at 370,000, and Soviet troops would leave by the end of 1994. On 3 October East Germany joined the Federal Republic. The last Russian troops left Germany at the end of August 1994.

The Soviet Union came apart just as fast. The Baltic states led the way in declaring their independence restored. In August 1991 hardliners attempted a coup; it failed, and republic after republic declared independence. On 8 December the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus signed an agreement founding the Commonwealth of Independent States. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December, and the next day the Soviet Union formally ceased to exist. The Warsaw Pact and Comecon were also dissolved that year.

Yugoslavia broke up in war. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991; Slovenia broke free after ten days of fighting, but the war in Croatia lasted until 1995. Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence in 1992 and was engulfed by an even more brutal war: Sarajevo was besieged for nearly four years, and by the time the fighting ended in 1995 about 100,000 people had died. Czechoslovakia's split was far calmer: on 1 January 1993 it divided peacefully in two, without a referendum. In the Caucasus, Armenia and Azerbaijan fought for years over Nagorno-Karabakh until a ceasefire in May 1994.
